docs.title: CitCom AI Trustworthiness Label
docs.text:
The CitCom AI Trustworthiness Label is a CitCom.ai service, currently under pilot, through which TEF site partners independently assess AI systems deployed in smart-city contexts — across mobility, energy, citizen services, urban planning, and related domains.

Its purpose is to provide a trusted, recognisable signal: an independent expert opinion on whether an AI system has been developed and operated responsibly for its intended use. The Label gives cities a sounder basis for procurement and gives providers a credible way to demonstrate responsible practice on the market.

Not a conformity certificate. The Label and its recommendations do not constitute a conformity certificate and are not legally binding — in particular, they are not a conformity assessment under the AI Act. The Label is an expert, evidence-based judgement, not a pass/fail certification. Its value lies in the independent third-party assessment itself, which builds trust between cities and providers and eases the procurement process.

docs.title: Who requests an assessment? Two streams
docs.text:
An assessment can be initiated from either side of the market. Both lead to the same independent process and the same kind of report.

Stream 1 — Municipality. A municipality needs to procure an AI solution but lacks the in-house capacity or competence to evaluate it. It requests an independent third-party assessment from a TEF site to support its procurement decision.

Stream 2 — AI provider. An AI provider requests the assessment voluntarily, so that its solution becomes more credible on the market and easier to recommend to public-sector buyers.

docs.title: How it works: the value proposition
docs.text:
A TEF site conducts the assessment as an independent domain expert and releases an assessment report. The TEF site is not auditing compliance against a standard — it is forming a professional, evidence-grounded opinion about whether the system has been developed and operated responsibly in its smart-city context.

The tangible outcome of the process is a system of badges. Each badge corresponds to a specific dimension of trustworthiness that was assessed. Badges are awarded independently — a provider may receive one, two, or all three — and receiving a badge on one dimension says nothing about the others.

Badge What it covers Technical Testing How the system was evaluated for trustworthiness: testing methodology, independence of testing, performance, fairness, robustness and failure modes, safety, and explainability. Governance The governance, oversight, and operational practices around the system: risk management, human oversight, accountability, monitoring and incident response, and documentation. Impact The effects of the system on people, communities, and society: affected populations, differential impact, transparency and recourse, broader societal effects, participation, and environmental footprint.

Each badge would include a watermark to ensure authenticity and prevent misuse, and would be verifiable through the CitCom Hub, allowing external stakeholders to confirm its origin and evaluation status.

docs.title: Customised to context and use case
docs.text: Each evaluation can focus on specific aspects and is customised to the deployment context and the actual use case of the AI system. The questions addressed for each badge represent a minimal set; a TEF site may add further ones where the specifics of the system or its smart-city context warrant it. This is what makes the assessment meaningful rather than a generic checklist.

docs.title: Consistency across TEF sites
docs.text:
Because each evaluation is customised — and because different TEF sites contribute different specialised expertise — it is essential that all sites follow the same guidelines. Shared guidelines are what keep the Label consistent and equally valuable wherever it is awarded, so that a badge means the same thing regardless of which TEF site issued it.

The two reference documents below define and illustrate that common approach:

  • Assessment Guidelines for TEF sites — how to conduct an assessment, what each badge covers, and how to exercise and document expert judgement consistently.
  • Example Assessment Report — a fully worked (fictional) report showing how the guidelines are applied in practice and how a finished report looks.

For the Technical Testing badge, one such resource is the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator, developed under the Luxembourg AI Factory. It offers a harmonised way of configuring and conducting the technical evaluation, and is suggested as one option among others — TEF sites remain free to apply their own methodologies and tools where these better fit the system and context.

docs.title: Multiple TEF sites for a single solution
docs.text: If a solution would benefit from complementary expertise available across several TEF sites, an AI provider can undergo assessments in multiple locations. In such cases, the first-contact TEF site coordinates the overall process: it connects with the additional sites (which assess independently), ensures each manages its own contractual and operational responsibilities, consolidates the results into a unified report, and oversees the issuance of the corresponding badges.

docs.title: How the data space works
docs.text: The CitCom data space is operated by VRAIN-UPV for the whole of CitCom and uses the FIWARE Data Space Connector (version 10), which follows the recommendations of the Data Spaces Business Alliance. This page describes its parts, the deployment running today and the four flows that make it work.

docs.title: Shared services
docs.text: Trust anchor Keeps the Trusted Issuers Registry (TIR): the list of organisations whose credentials are trusted in the data space, by their decentralised identifier (did:web:…). A verifier rejects any credential issued by an organisation that is not in it. Onboarding portal Where an organisation asks to join. Its legal representative (LEAR) registers the organisation; once approved, it is added to the trust anchor, and the LEAR acts for it with a LegalPersonCredential. Marketplace The catalogue of offers, built on the TM Forum APIs and the BAE frontend. The LEAR of each organisation logs in with a wallet, sets up the organisation's profile, publishes offers and buys them. See Marketplace.

docs.title: Inside a connector
docs.text:
Every participant runs the same set of components:

flowchart LR
    subgraph CON["Connector of a participant"]
        direction LR
        KC["<b>Keycloak</b><br/>issues credentials<br/>(OID4VCI)"]
        VF["<b>Verifier</b><br/>credential → token<br/>(OID4VP)"]
        TIL[("<b>Trusted Issuers List</b><br/>who may access")]
        GW["<b>APISIX</b><br/>gateway"]
        OPA["<b>OPA</b><br/>policy decision"]
        PAP[("<b>ODRL-PAP</b><br/>access policies")]
        CM["<b>contract-management</b><br/>applies purchases"]
        BR[("<b>NGSI-LD broker</b><br/>Scorpio / Orion-LD / Lepus")]
        VF --> TIL
        GW --> OPA --> PAP
        GW --> BR
        CM --> TIL
        CM --> PAP
    end
    CLIENT["Consumer"] -- "1 credential" --> VF
    CLIENT -- "2 token + request" --> GW
    MKT["Marketplace"] -- "completed order" --> CM
Component Role Keycloak Identity server of the organisation. Issues MachineCredential and ServiceCredential to its programs and people with OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance (OID4VCI), as SD-JWT credentials. Verifier Receives credentials from consumers (OpenID for Verifiable Presentations), checks them against the trust anchor and the local trust list, and returns an access token. Trusted Issuers List (TIL) The organisations allowed to access this connector, per credential type and role. Filled in when someone buys an offer. APISIX The gateway in front of the data and services. Checks the token and asks OPA for a decision on every request. OPA + ODRL-PAP The policy engine. The PAP stores ODRL policies and turns them into rules for OPA, which allows or denies each request by organisation, path, entity type and method. contract-management Listens to the marketplace. When an order for one of this participant's offers is completed, it adds the buyer to the TIL and loads the offer's policy into the PAP. NGSI-LD broker The data itself. Scorpio comes with the connector; the Ajuntament also serves its data through Orion-LD and Lepus.

docs.title: Join the data space
docs.text:
1. The organisation's LEAR registers it in the onboarding portal.
  2. Once approved, the organisation's did:web is added to the trust anchor.
  3. The LEAR logs in to the marketplace with a wallet and completes the organisation's profile. A provider also sets the address of its contract-management there, so purchases reach its connector.

The guide Join the data space has the details.

docs.title: A machine reads data
docs.text:
This is how a program, such as the MIAIS, reads data from another organisation. The library ds-consumer-auth does steps 1 to 4 for you.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant APP as Consumer program
    participant KC as Consumer Keycloak
    participant VF as Provider verifier
    participant GW as Provider APISIX
    participant OPA as Provider OPA
    participant BR as Provider broker
    APP->>KC: Log in and request a MachineCredential (OID4VCI)
    KC-->>APP: Signed credential (SD-JWT)
    APP->>VF: Present the credential (vp_token)
    VF->>VF: Issuer in the trust anchor? Consumer in the TIL with these roles?
    VF-->>APP: Access token (short-lived JWT)
    APP->>GW: GET /ngsi-ld/v1/entities?type=WasteContainer + token
    GW->>OPA: Allowed?
    OPA-->>GW: Yes, a purchased policy matches
    GW->>BR: Forward
    BR-->>APP: Entities (NGSI-LD)

If the consumer has not bought any offer, step 5 fails: the verifier does not find the consumer in its TIL. If it has bought an offer but not this dataset, step 8 fails: no policy allows that entity type. See Use data from your code.

docs.title: A person uses a web service
docs.text:
A provider can also offer a web application. People log in with a wallet instead of a password, and the provider's gateway does the login: the application needs no login code of its own.

sequenceDiagram

    actor U as Person with a wallet
    participant GW as Provider APISIX
    participant VF as Provider verifier
    participant OPA as Provider OPA
    participant APP as Web service (e.g. MIAIS)
    U->>GW: Open https://waste-collection-vrain.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu
    GW-->>U: No session: redirect to the verifier
    VF-->>U: QR code
    U->>VF: Scan with the wallet, present the ServiceCredential
    VF->>VF: Issuer trusted? Organisation bought the service, with this role?
    VF-->>GW: Authorisation code → token
    GW-->>U: Encrypted session cookie
    U->>GW: Requests with the session
    GW->>OPA: Allowed? (path /waste-collection, role)
    GW->>APP: Forward

The person's organisation must have bought the service, and the person must have the role the service asks for in their ServiceCredential. See Publish a web service.

docs.title: Eclipse EDC data space
docs.text: Besides the CitCom data space, some partners use a separate data space built on the Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC). It is operated by Libelium at citcom.dataspaceready.eu and lets organisations publish data assets, discover the assets of other participants, negotiate machine-readable usage policies and exchange the data under those agreements.

docs.title: The stack
docs.text:
• Connectors: Eclipse EDC, through the sovity Community Edition 16.4.2 distribution, which adds management interfaces and defaults but stays compatible with upstream EDC.
  • Management portal: DS-Manager, by Hopu, the human-facing side: identity, asset metadata, policy drafting, catalogue browsing and audit. It talks to the connectors through the EDC Management API.
  • Protocol: the Dataspace Protocol (DSP) for catalogues, contract negotiation and transfers between connectors.

CitCom is one of four data spaces built on the same platform; each one is a thin per-project layer over a shared core.

docs.title: 1. Scope and positioning
docs.text:
CitCom.ai is a multi-tenant data space that lets organisations publish data assets, discover assets published by other participants, negotiate machine-readable usage policies, and exchange the data under those agreements.

It is built on the Eclipse Dataspace Components (EDC) open-source project (Eclipse Foundation), which we deploy through the Sovity Community Edition 16.4.2 distribution (ghcr.io/sovity/edc-ce:16.4.2). On top of EDC, we layer:

  • DS-Manager — backend (FastAPI) + frontend (React) by Hopu (registry.hopu.eu/dsr-backend:1.3.4-generic-ds, registry.hopu.eu/dsr-frontend:1.3.3-generic-ds). DS-Manager is the human-facing management plane: identity, asset metadata, policy drafting, federated catalogue browsing, audit. It speaks to EDC over EDC's Management API. Container names and Keycloak identifiers carry the legacy dsr-* prefix (Hopu's original "Data Space Ready" brand); we keep those verbatim everywhere they're a runtime literal.
  • An onboarding portal (onboarding-api, Flask) for tenant registration, the participant registry and SMTP delivery of activation emails.
  • A federated catalogue. Two interchangeable backends are supported and the choice is per–data-space (CATALOG_BACKEND env): DCAT in Apache Jena Fuseki for SPARQL access, or TMForum/DOME product offerings in Scorpio NGSI-LD for a marketplace-style browse UX. CitCom is wired to the DOME stack (CATALOG_BACKEND=tmforum). Both pipelines are populated by sync workers that poll every connector's EDC catalogue every 30–60 s.
  • Object storage (MinIO, S3-compatible) with a per-tenant bucket served behind an authenticated portal.
  • Identity anchored on Keycloak as the OIDC issuer, plus DS-Manager-level DIDs (did:web:<subdomain>.<domain>:did:<uuid>) for participants and per-tenant LEAR designations.
  • Reverse proxy + TLS via Traefik, with per-host Let's Encrypt certificates issued through the Cloudflare DNS-01 challenge.

The result is a deployment where each tenant gets its own subdomain, its own EDC connector, its own DS-Manager instance (so policy state and audit are tenant-isolated), and its own MinIO bucket, but shares the Keycloak realm, the catalogue index and the onboarding landing page.

docs.title: 3. The Eclipse EDC role
docs.text:
For each tenant we run one EDC connector (cp-{tenant}), based on ghcr.io/sovity/edc-ce:16.4.2. The connector exposes four HTTP endpoint groups, each on its own port:

Group Port Purpose Who calls it Management 8181 Asset / policy / contract definition / catalogue / negotiation / transfer CRUD DS-Manager backend, sync workers, deploy scripts Protocol (DSP) 9084 Eclipse Dataspace Protocol — federated catalogue, contract negotiation, transfer authorisation Other connectors Public (data plane) 9006 Bearer-protected data egress for HttpData-PULL transfers Consumer once it has an EDR Control 9241 Internal control plane (data-plane-management) Connector internals only

The connector is configured in pure code (no UI of its own); we drive it from DS-Manager.

docs.title: What runs inside an EDC connector
docs.text:
• DSP catalog — answers dcat:Catalog queries with the connector's visible offerings. Each dcat:dataset carries a dcat:distribution list (HttpData-PULL, HttpData-PUSH, S3-PUSH, AzureStorage-PUSH) and an odrl:hasPolicy referring to the associated ContractDefinition.
  • Contract negotiation — implements the Dataspace Protocol state machine (REQUESTED → AGREED/VERIFIED → FINALIZED). Validates that the offer the consumer requests matches what's in the catalogue (offer policy, target asset, assigner).
  • Transfer process — once a contract is finalized, allocates an EDR (Endpoint Data Reference) — a one-time bearer token + URL that the consumer uses to pull the data plane.
  • Data plane — for HttpData-PULL, fronts the asset's dataAddress (HTTP, S3, etc.) so the consumer never sees the raw storage credentials.

docs.title: Data addresses we currently support
docs.text:
AssetCreate requests in DS-Manager map straight to EDC dataAddress fields. The most common shapes:

  • HttpData (open or with bearer/apiKey auth) — the asset is served from any HTTP endpoint reachable by the provider connector.
  • AmazonS3 — the asset lives in an S3-compatible bucket. We use endpointOverride: http://minio:9000 to target the in-cluster MinIO.
  • The internal http://storage/edc/{tenant}/{object} URL — a shorter-form HttpData address served by the storage portal's internal /edc/<tenant>/... route. Reachable only from the docker network so it never leaks outside the data plane.

docs.title: 4. Federated catalogue
docs.text:
The platform supports two interchangeable catalogue backends, both populated by polling each connector's EDC catalogue every 30–60 s. The choice is per–data-space, set with CATALOG_BACKEND in the project's env.<env> file:

Value Index Browsable from Use when sparql Apache Jena Fuseki + DCAT (one named graph per tenant) /catalog/ connector-ui (SPARQL UI) Audience is data-engineering / RDF-native; you want raw SPARQL access to the federated metadata. tmforum Scorpio NGSI-LD + TMForum APIs (TMF620 productCatalog, TMF634 resourceCatalog, TMF638 serviceCatalog) /dome-catalog/ BAE marketplace UI + /catalog/ connector-ui in TMForum mode Audience is a marketplace / business user; you want a richer browse + filter UX and TMForum-shaped product offerings.

The two are functionally redundant — every dataset that reaches one also reaches the other if both are wired up — but in practice each deployment picks the one that matches its audience.

CitCom is configured with CATALOG_BACKEND=tmforum, so the active federated catalogue is the DOME stack (Scorpio NGSI-LD + the TMForum API gateway in front of it, with the BAE marketplace UI as the human-facing browser at https://citcom.dataspaceready.eu/dome-catalog/).

The Fuseki/SPARQL pipeline (4.1 below) still runs in the cluster as a fallback / engineering surface — it's cheap and useful for debugging — but it is not what citcom users see.

docs.title: 4.1 TMForum / DOME (active in CitCom)
docs.text:
A worker (sync-dome, Node.js, every 60 s by default) walks each connector listed in the participant registry, fetches its DCAT catalogue via DSP, maps each dataset to a TMForum triplet ResourceSpecification → ProductSpecification → ProductOffering, and upserts the result into the TMForum API gateway in front of the Scorpio NGSI-LD broker. The same worker also reports its liveness to onboarding-api's /sync-status so the catalogue page shows "last updated s ago" to the user. 

sequenceDiagram
  participant SD as sync-dome<br/>(Node.js, every 60 s)
  participant Reg as Registry<br/>(onboarding-api)
  participant E_a as EDC admin<br/>(requester)
  participant E_t as EDC tenant<br/>(target)
  participant TMF as TMForum API<br/>(Scorpio NGSI-LD)
  participant BAE as BAE marketplace<br/>UI
  SD->>Reg: GET /registry
  Reg-->>SD: participants[]
  loop for each participant
    SD->>E_a: POST /catalog/request<br/>{counterPartyAddress: target DSP}
    E_a->>E_t: DSP catalog request
    E_t-->>E_a: dcat:Catalog
    E_a-->>SD: dcat:Catalog
    SD->>TMF: upsert ResourceSpec → ProductSpec → ProductOffering<br/>(TMF634 / TMF620)
  end
  BAE->>TMF: GET /productOffering<br/>(browser query)
  TMF-->>BAE: filtered list

Human-facing browser: the BAE / DOME marketplace at https://citcom.dataspaceready.eu/dome-catalog/ (and a TMForum-mode build of connector-ui at /catalog/ that hits the same TMForum API endpoints rather than SPARQL).

docs.title: 4.2 DCAT / SPARQL (Apache Jena Fuseki — alternative backend)
docs.text:
This is the path you'd pick if your audience is RDF-native or you want a programmable SPARQL surface across the whole data space. CitCom doesn't expose this to end users, but the pipeline runs in the cluster as a parallel index — useful for debugging and as a fallback.

sequenceDiagram
  participant SS as sync-service<br/>(Node.js, every 30 s)
  participant Reg as Registry<br/>(onboarding-api)
  participant E_a as EDC admin<br/>(requester)
  participant E_t as EDC tenant<br/>(target)
  participant F as Fuseki<br/>(named graphs)
  SS->>Reg: GET /registry
  Reg-->>SS: participants[]
  loop for each participant
    SS->>E_a: POST /catalog/request<br/>{counterPartyAddress: target DSP}
    E_a->>E_t: DSP catalog request
    E_t-->>E_a: dcat:Catalog
    E_a-->>SS: dcat:Catalog
    SS->>F: SPARQL UPDATE<br/>graph http://dataspace/{tenant}/catalog
  end

When a project sets CATALOG_BACKEND=sparql, the connector-ui at /catalog/ switches to a SPARQL-mode build that issues federated queries directly against Fuseki for the union of all tenant graphs.

docs.title: 5. Identity model
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  subgraph kc[Keycloak realm DSR]
    direction TB
    DSRAPP[client: dsr-app<br/>shared template]
    DSRTLIB[client: dsr-app-libelium<br/>confidential]
    DSRTVAL[client: dsr-app-valencia<br/>confidential]
    DSRTUPV[client: dsr-app-upv<br/>confidential]
    PORTAL[client: ds-portal<br/>onboarding portal]
    USERS[Users in groups<br/>libelium, valencia, upv<br/>roles: dsr:asset-owner, dsr:operator]
  end

  subgraph dsr_t[DS-Manager per tenant]
    direction TB
    DID["/api/v1/dids/<br/>did:web:<subdomain>.<domain>:did:<uuid>"]
    ORG["/api/v1/orgs/<br/>org_id, legal_name, headquarter_address"]
    LEAR["/api/v1/orgs/<id>/lear<br/>designates user_did → org"]
  end

  USERS -->|password grant| DSRTLIB
  DSRTLIB -->|access_token| dsr_t
  dsr_t --> DID
  dsr_t --> ORG
  dsr_t --> LEAR
  • Keycloak is the identity issuer. It hosts a single realm (DSR), one shared template client (dsr-app) used by the portal, one confidential client per tenant (dsr-app-{tenant}) used by that tenant's DS-Manager backend, and a ds-portal client for the main-domain portal.
  • The per-tenant client is provisioned automatically by provision-tenant.py and kept in sync (mappers, scopes, flags) with dsr-app on every re-run.
  • DS-Manager DIDs are filesystem-style did:web: documents served from /did/<id>/x509CertificateChain.pem. Every user gets a personal DID; every Org gets one too. The LEAR (Legal Entity Appointed Representative) link maps a user DID to an org DID, which is what a consumer's connector verifies during contract negotiation.

docs.title: 6. Transfer flow (the path Albufera CSV took)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Libelium DS-Manager<br/>(consumer)
  participant EL as EDC libelium
  participant EV as EDC valencia
  participant V as Valencia DS-Manager<br/>(provider)
  participant M as MinIO
  L->>EL: POST /catalog/request<br/>(target: valencia DSP)
  EL->>EV: DSP catalog request
  EV-->>EL: dcat:Catalog<br/>{Albufera water level (15-min)}
  EL-->>L: catalogue with offer policy
  L->>EL: POST /contractnegotiations<br/>{policy verbatim from offer}
  EL->>EV: DSP contract request
  EV-->>EL: AGREED → VERIFIED → FINALIZED
  L->>EL: POST /transferprocesses<br/>{contractId, HttpData-PULL}
  EL->>EV: DSP transfer request
  EV->>EL: EDR (endpoint, bearer, expiry)
  L->>EL: POST /edrs/request → GET /edrs/{tp}/dataaddress
  EL-->>L: {endpoint: http://cp-valencia:9006/api/public, authorization: …}
  L->>EV: GET /api/public + Authorization: bearer
  EV->>M: read object via dataAddress
  M-->>EV: stream
  EV-->>L: stream (CSV bytes)

See diagrams/transfer-flow.excalidraw for an editable version of the same sequence.

Two notes from the implementation:

  1. The policy block sent in POST /contractnegotiations MUST include odrl: JSON-LD prefixes (@type: odrl:Offer, odrl:target, odrl:assigner). If you ship it under the EDC default @vocab, EDC validates @type as https://w3id.org/edc/v0.0.1/ns/Offer and rejects.
  2. The provider uses the consumer's verified DID/Org as the input to policy evaluation. With our open albufera-open-use policy (USE-only, no constraints) any verified consumer of any participant passes. With ABAC policies you can restrict per-attribute (LEAR, organisation country, etc.).

docs.title: 7. Per-tenant data isolation
docs.text: Layer Mechanism HTTP routing One nginx-{tenant} per subdomain; tenant-validator calls strict mode for the storage portal so a session for tenant A cannot read tenant B's bucket. Storage nginx-tenant.conf injects X-Participant: {tenant} so the storage-portal serves only that bucket. Internal /edc/<tenant>/ routes are blocked at the public gateway and only reachable from the docker network. Identity DS-Manager backend authenticates against dsr-app-{tenant} confidential client; resource_access.dsr-app-{tenant}.roles is the only role path it trusts. Catalog Sync workers write each tenant's catalogue to its own SPARQL named graph and its own TMForum tenant header. Database One dsr-postgres-{tenant} and one db-{tenant} (EDC). Per-tenant compose generated by provision-tenant.py.

docs.title: Eclipse EDC data space: deployment
docs.text: This is the operational guide for the CitCom data space at https://citcom.dataspaceready.eu. It assumes you've read architecture.md for the what; this doc focuses on the how.

docs.title: 1. Topology
docs.text:
flowchart LR

  end
  CF -->|443| Traefik

  • Server: 145.239.127.76 (citcom-ds), Ubuntu, user ubuntu.
  • Deploy directory: ~/citcom/ (rsync target — not a git worktree).
  • Single Docker network: edc-net (external; created on first deploy).
  • Persistent state: Docker volumes for each Postgres and MinIO instance + the Traefik ACME store.
  • DNS: Wildcard *.citcom.dataspaceready.eu in Cloudflare → host IP. The traefik-cloudflare-companion sidecar registers any new Traefik host label automatically, so a new tenant subdomain resolves without manual DNS work.
  • TLS: Per-host Let's Encrypt certs via the Cloudflare DNS-01 challenge (no port-80 challenge → wildcard-friendly + does not break HTTP→HTTPS redirect).

docs.title: 2. The deploy command
docs.text:
A full deploy from a developer machine is one line:

make deploy-prod-remote PROJECT=citcom

What it does:

  1. rsync the repo (excluding .git/, active/, secrets) to ubuntu@citcom-ds:~/citcom/.
  2. ssh into the host and run make deploy-prod PROJECT=citcom, which is a thin wrapper for make deploy ENV=production PROJECT=citcom SSL=skip.
  3. smoke test with curl https://citcom.dataspaceready.eu/.

The make deploy target itself does, in order:

  1. make activate — render active/ from platform/ + projects/citcom/
  2. env.production + tenants.yml. This regenerates active/keycloak/realm-export.json, every tenant compose under active/tenants/, the Keycloak theme, the navbar config, etc.
  3. Fix file permissions (chmod -R o+rX active/) so containers can read bind-mounted assets.
  4. Pull all images referenced by every compose file. Hopu re-publishes 1.3.x-generic-ds regularly with the same tag, so a blind docker compose up -d would silently keep the old digest; we explicitly pull first.
  5. Bring up the platform: Traefik (with docker-compose.cloudflare.yml and docker-compose.traefik-le.yml overlays when CLOUDFLARE_ENABLED=true), then docker-compose.yml, then MinIO (docker-compose-minio.yml), then the admin connector (docker-compose-tenant-admin.yml), then every per-tenant compose under active/tenants/.
  6. Force-recreate every nginx gateway. Their config is bind-mounted from active/nginx/*.conf.template so a vanilla up -d doesn't pick up template changes.
  7. Force-recreate Keycloak. Same bind-mount problem (the themes directory and realm-export.json are mounted; make activate removes and recreates those files, so the inode under the old container is stale).
  8. Bring up the audit pipeline (Loki + Alloy).
  9. Run keycloak_sync.py (self-heal). Reconciles realm-level fields, mappers and per-client redirect URIs against active/keycloak/realm-export.json. Self-heals admin password drift via fallback-and-rotate. Idempotent — second run is a no-op.
  10. Run register-admin-connector.py to ensure the admin connector exists in the admin DS-Manager's connector_registry.ds_connector.
  11. Print URLs and exit.

docs.title: 3. Provisioning a new tenant
docs.text:
Tenants are declared in tenants.yml. Each entry covers identity, EDC, contact, users and (optional but recommended) org_details for the DS-Manager Organisation registry:

- name: libelium             # used as connector / db / k8s-style identifier
  subdomain: libelium        # https://libelium.citcom.dataspaceready.eu
  org: Libelium              # display name
  sector: Technology
  contact:
    name: Mateo Ferri
    email: m.ferri@libelium.com
    role: Data Engineer
  edc:
    api_key: api-key-libelium  # X-Api-Key for the connector's management API
    public_port: 9005          # internal port for the connector's data plane
  org_details:
    vat: ESB99065815
    street: Calle Bari 19, Edificio CEEI
    city: Zaragoza
    postal: "50197"
    subdivision: ES-Z          # ISO-3166-2 — the DS-Manager backend rejects anything else
    country: ES
  users:
    - email: m.ferri@libelium.com
      password: ...
      first_name: Mateo
      last_name: Ferri
      roles: [dsr:asset-owner, dsr:operator]

Then:

# After editing tenants.yml on a deployed host:
cd ~/citcom
ln -sf active/env env                      # provision-tenant.py reads cwd/env
ln -sf active/tenants.yml tenants.yml      # ... and cwd/tenants.yml
python3 platform/scripts/provision-tenant.py <tenant-name> --skip-verify
# or do all at once:
python3 platform/scripts/provision-tenant.py --all --skip-verify

provision-tenant.py performs 9 idempotent steps per tenant:

  1. Generate active/tenants/docker-compose-tenant-<name>.yml.
  2. Add the tenant subdomain to the dsr-app redirect URIs.
  3. Create or self-heal the per-tenant OIDC client (dsr-app-<name>) — re-applies all 5 protocol mappers and copies the 8 default + 1 optional client scopes from dsr-app even when the client already exists, fixing accumulated drift.
  4. Start the tenant containers (or --skip-containers if they're already up after a make deploy).
  5. Create the Keycloak group + each declared user, attach roles.
  6. Register the EDC connector in the tenant DS-Manager's connector_registry.ds_connector (HTTP API first, falls back to direct Postgres insert).
  7. Identity setup (DID + Organisation + LEAR designation). This step runs inside the onboarding-api container so all the HTTP calls resolve through the internal Docker DNS — running on the host silently fails because the public domain doesn't loop back.
  8. Add the new connector's catalogue endpoints to the sync-service compose so the federated catalogue picks it up.
  9. Endpoint smoke check (skipped with --skip-verify).

docs.title: 4. Self-healing
docs.text:
Two self-healers run on every deploy:

  • platform/scripts/keycloak_sync.py — reconciles the running Keycloak realm with the rendered active/keycloak/realm-export.json (themes, SMTP, locale, mappers, redirect URIs). Auto-rotates the admin password if the value in env.production no longer authenticates and a known fallback (e.g. admin) does.
  • platform/onboarding-api/register-admin-connector.py — ensures the admin EDC connector is registered in the admin DS-Manager's connector_registry.ds_connector. SQL-direct (the previous /test-auth/create-session endpoint was removed in dsr-backend 1.3.4).

Both are idempotent and non-fatal: a deploy succeeds even if either fails.

docs.title: 6. Self-issued certificates
docs.text:
The Traefik service is configured to issue per-host certs through the Cloudflare DNS-01 challenge. The flag chain:

--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.email=...
--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.storage=/acme/acme.json
--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.dnschallenge=true
--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.dnschallenge.provider=cloudflare
--certificatesresolvers.le.acme.dnschallenge.resolvers=1.1.1.1:53,8.8.8.8:53

Each routed service ships a label traefik.http.routers.<name>.tls.certresolver=${TRAEFIK_CERTRESOLVER:-}, which evaluates to le in production (where the env sets it) and to empty in local dev (where Traefik falls back to the file provider's self-signed wildcard). Adding a new tenant therefore needs no manual cert work — Traefik issues one on the first request to its host.

docs.title: 7. SMTP / email
docs.text:
onboarding-api sends activation emails directly through SMTP (it does not delegate to Keycloak's mailing). Production points at smtp.buzondecorreo.com:465 SSL, authenticated as info@geospace.es — recipients see the message as From: CitCom.ai <info@geospace.es>. The HTML template lives at platform/onboarding-api/templates/activation-email.html and is parametrised entirely from env (EMAIL_PRIMARY_COLOR, EMAIL_ACCENT_COLOR, EMAIL_LOGO_FILE, …) so each project's emails match its login + portal palette.

Caveat — sender domain (geospace.es) does not match the data- space domain (citcom.dataspaceready.eu), so a strict DMARC policy at the recipient's MX may quarantine. Long-term we'll set up noreply@citcom.dataspaceready.eu with proper SPF/DKIM in Cloudflare; short-term Mailpit on mailpit.citcom.dataspaceready.eu remains as a debug surface.

docs.title: Add a tenant
docs.text:
1. Append entry to projects/citcom/tenants.yml.
  2. make deploy-prod-remote PROJECT=citcom (or, if you only want the tenant change without a full redeploy, ssh in and python3 platform/scripts/provision-tenant.py <new-tenant>).
  3. Activation emails are NOT sent automatically by provisioning — they are sent by an explicit call to the onboarding-api's send_activation helper. We dispatch them in batch after provisioning completes (see the in-session ad-hoc script we used the day of go-live).

docs.title: Rotate the Keycloak admin password
docs.text:
1. Edit KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD in projects/citcom/env.production.
  2. make deploy-prod-remote PROJECT=citcom.
  3. keycloak_sync.py detects the env doesn't authenticate, falls back to the prior known password, resets the master admin user to the new env value.
  4. Save the new password to a secrets store (memory, vault, …) and update memory/citcom_keycloak_admin.md.

docs.title: Refresh DS-Manager images
docs.text: Because Hopu re-tags 1.3.x-generic-ds, a redeploy is enough — the deploy target now does an explicit docker compose pull before up -d. Force-recreate of the relevant containers happens automatically.

docs.title: Diagnose a failing transfer
docs.text:
1. Provider EDC log: docker logs cp-<provider-tenant> --tail 200 — look for ContractNegotiation: ID … Fatal error lines. The most common one is the JSON-LD policy mismatch on POST /contractnegotiations.
  2. Consumer side: GET /api/management/v3/contractnegotiations/<id> shows the state machine; state=TERMINATED plus errorDetail tells you what the consumer rejected.
  3. EDR phase: GET /api/management/v3/edrs/{transferProcessId}/dataaddress returns the bearer token + endpoint. If that endpoint 401s, the token expired or the data-plane URL is wrong.

docs.title: 9. Known runtime drift / things to watch
docs.text:
• The realm-import lifecycle in Keycloak applies once. Without keycloak_sync.py, every theme / SMTP / mapper change after first import is silently ignored.
  • Tag-pinned images can drift under the same tag. The deploy target now docker compose pulls explicitly to defeat this.
  • nginx + Keycloak both bind-mount files that make activate regenerates → --force-recreate is on by default for those services.
  • org_details.subdivision MUST match ^[A-Z]{2}-[A-Z0-9]{1,3}$ or the DS-Manager Organisation API rejects with a cryptic 422.

docs.title: 10. Evidence the data space is operational (last verified 2026-04-29)
docs.text:
• Federated DCAT catalogue from libelium → valencia DSP returns the Albufera dataset.
  • Contract negotiation 019dd641-… reaches FINALIZED.
  • Transfer process 019dd641-… reaches STARTED; EDR endpoint http://cp-valencia:9006/api/public issued with a 1-time bearer.
  • Consumer GET of that endpoint returns the 2 022 698-byte CSV (dateObserved,numValue,…) — i.e. the actual asset bytes flow end-to-end through Eclipse EDC's DSP + data plane.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: What CitCom.ai is and why its technical pieces fit together the way they do, in plain words. Start here if you are new to the project: each page is short and leads to the deeper chapters.

docs.title: CitCom in four questions
docs.text:
• What is it?

    A European Union project that runs Testing and Experimentation Facilities (TEFs) for AI and robotics in smart cities. Companies test their AI products in real cities, with real data, before they reach the market.

    The project and the TEFs

  • What does it build on?

    The European work on data sharing between cities: the Minimal Interoperability Mechanisms (MIMs) of OASC, Smart Data Models, and the data space recommendations of the DSSC and DS4SSCC.

    Interoperability

  • Which technology does it use?

    NGSI-LD brokers to serve the data, Smart Data Models to describe it, and a data space built with FIWARE to share it under control, with verifiable credentials held in a wallet.

    Data spaces in 5 minutes

  • Who provides what?

    The TEF nodes offer their services to AI and robotics innovators. CitCom's work package 3 (WP3) offers the TEF nodes a minimal package: a common reference architecture, with the guides, tools and deployment examples to apply it. This hub gathers it.

    The minimal package

docs.title: Data spaces in 5 minutes
docs.text:
A data space is a set of rules and software that lets organisations share data while each one keeps control of its own. There is no central database: the data stays with its provider, and the provider decides who can read it and under which conditions.

This page explains the few concepts you need to follow the rest of the site. The CitCom data space is built on them; How it works shows how they are implemented.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    TA["<b>Trust anchor</b><br/>who belongs to the data space"]
    MK["<b>Marketplace</b><br/>offers and contracts"]
    subgraph P["Provider"]
        PC["Connector"] --- PD[("Data")]
    end
    subgraph C["Consumer"]
        CC["Connector or app"] --- W["Wallet / credentials"]
    end
    P -. "registered in" .-> TA
    C -. "registered in" .-> TA
    P -- "publishes an offer" --> MK
    C -- "buys the offer" --> MK
    C == "reads the data<br/>with a credential" ==> PC
Participant An organisation in the data space: a city council, a company, a university. In CitCom, for example, the Ajuntament de València (townhall-vlc) and VRAIN-UPV (vrain). A participant can be a provider (offers data or services), a consumer (uses them), or both. Trust anchor The list of participants that everyone trusts. When an organisation joins, the operator of the data space adds it to the trust anchor. From then on, the credentials it issues are accepted by the others. Connector The software each participant runs at its border. For a provider, it sits in front of the data: it checks who is asking, applies the access rules and only then forwards the request. In CitCom it is the FIWARE Data Space Connector. Verifiable credential

A digital certificate, signed by an organisation, that says something about a person or a machine: "this is an employee of VRAIN", "this program acts for VRAIN with the role clearence1". People keep theirs in a wallet on the phone or the desktop; programs request them from their organisation's identity server. CitCom uses three types:

Credential Held by Used to LegalPersonCredential the legal representative (LEAR) of an organisation act for the organisation: join, buy, sell MachineCredential a program read data through an API ServiceCredential a person log in to a web service offered in the data space Offer What a provider makes available: a dataset or a service, with a description, terms of use and the access rule it grants. Offers are published in the marketplace, where anyone can browse them. Contract and policy When a consumer buys an offer, a contract is created. The provider's connector then registers two things: that the consumer's credentials are now accepted, and an access policy (written in ODRL) that says exactly what they can read, for example "only WasteContainer entities, only through this path".

docs.title: What happens when a consumer reads data
docs.text:
1. The consumer buys the offer in the marketplace. The provider's connector registers the contract.
  2. The consumer's program gets a MachineCredential from its own organisation.
  3. It presents the credential to the provider's connector and receives a short-lived access token.
  4. It calls the data API with that token. The connector checks the policy and returns the data.

Nobody shares passwords, and the provider never creates accounts for consumers: trust comes from the trust anchor, and access from the contract. The FIWARE data space page shows these steps as diagrams.

docs.title: Why not just an API key?
docs.text:
An API key works between two organisations that already know each other. A data space works between many organisations that do not, and gives each provider:

  • sovereignty: the data stays at home and the provider writes the rules;
  • traceability: every access is tied to an organisation and a contract;
  • scale: a new consumer does not need a new account or a new integration, only a purchase.

Further reading

  • Data Spaces Support Centre: the European reference on data spaces and their building blocks.
  • DS4SSCC: data spaces for smart and sustainable cities and communities.
  • FIWARE Data Space Connector and Eclipse Dataspace Components.

docs.title: Interoperability
docs.text: Interoperability is what lets a service built for one city run in another city without a new integration. CitCom measures it with a simple ladder of three levels, built on the Minimal Interoperability Mechanisms.

docs.title: MIMs
docs.text:
The Minimal Interoperability Mechanisms (MIMs) are a small set of agreements, published by Open & Agile Smart Cities (OASC), that cities adopt so their systems can talk to each other. They are minimal on purpose: a city does not replace its platform, it adds a common interface on top. CitCom uses two of them as its base:

MIM What it fixes In CitCom MIM1 Context information management One API to read and write data about real-world entities NGSI-LD, served by a context broker (Orion-LD, Scorpio) MIM2 Data models One vocabulary to describe those entities Smart Data Models, such as WasteContainer or AirQualityObserved

docs.title: Interoperability levels
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    L0["<b>Level 0</b><br/>Custom integration<br/><i>one adapter per city</i>"]
    L1["<b>Level 1</b><br/>NGSI-LD + Smart Data Models<br/><i>same API and models everywhere</i>"]
    L2["<b>Level 2</b><br/>Data space<br/><i>same API, plus trust and access control</i>"]
    L0 -- "adopt MIM1 + MIM2" --> L1
    L1 -- "add a connector" --> L2

docs.title: Level 0: custom integration
docs.text: There is no common standard. Each platform is connected with an integration written for it: its own API, its own field names, its own authentication. It works, but every new city means a new integration, and the data cannot be reused easily by others.

docs.title: Level 1: pivotal interoperability points
docs.text:
The platform exposes its data through NGSI-LD (MIM1) and describes it with Smart Data Models (MIM2). The platform can keep its own internals: what matters is that the interface is the same. A service written for level 1 reads waste containers in Valencia and in any other level-1 city with the same code.

What is still missing is control: a level-1 broker is usually either open to everyone or protected with an ad hoc key.

docs.title: Level 2: common interface with integrated security
docs.text:
The NGSI-LD interface is placed behind a data space connector. Level 1 stays as it is, and the connector adds what is needed to share data between organisations that do not know each other in advance:

  • a trust framework: who belongs to the data space, managed by a trust anchor;
  • identity: each organisation, person and machine proves who it is with verifiable credentials;
  • authorisation: access rules (ODRL policies) that the provider defines and the connector enforces, usually created when a consumer buys an offer in the marketplace.

Data spaces in 5 minutes explains these pieces.

docs.title: The levels in practice
docs.text:
The MIAIS, the worked example of this site, has one version per level. Its code shows what really changes from one level to the next:

Level How the MIAIS gets the waste containers 0 From a custom API of the city platform 1 From an NGSI-LD broker, as WasteContainer entities 2 From the same NGSI-LD API, through the Valencia connector, after buying the offer in the marketplace and presenting a credential

For a city that already runs an NGSI-v2 platform, Lepus is a shortcut to level 1: it serves the NGSI-v2 data as NGSI-LD without migrating the platform. Valencia uses it this way.

Learn more

  • OASC: MIMs Plus and the MIMs toolkit.
  • IDSA: Interoperability in data spaces, with its four layers: technical, semantic, organisational and legal.

docs.title: What a TEF is
docs.text:
A Testing and Experimentation Facility (TEF) is a place where companies test AI and robotics products in real conditions before they reach the market. The European Commission funds TEFs in several sectors; CitCom.ai is the one for smart and sustainable cities and communities.

In practice, a CitCom TEF site is a city, a living lab or a research centre that offers:

  • Real environments: streets, buildings, energy grids or mobility hubs where a product can run.
  • Data: city platforms with sensor and open data, increasingly shared through a data space.
  • Expertise: help to scope the test, check regulatory compliance (GDPR, the AI Act, cybersecurity) and assess the result.

The project brings together more than 30 organisations in 11 EU countries. The CitCom TEF website is the entry point for companies that want to test a product.

docs.title: Three super-nodes
docs.text:
The sites are grouped in three super-nodes, each with a theme. A super-node is a regional hub that shares expertise and resources between its sites.

Nordic Central South Theme POWER MOVE CONNECT Focus Energy, environment, cybersecurity, ethics, edge learning Mobility and logistics Securely connecting citizens, infrastructure, AI and robotics across city services Lead Denmark Belgium Spain Countries Denmark, Sweden, Finland Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands Spain, Italy, Poland, Germany

Every site has its own page in the TEF network.

docs.title: Why a common architecture
docs.text:
Each city already has its own data platform, often built years ago with its own interfaces. A product tested in one city would need a new integration in the next one. CitCom avoids that by agreeing on a few common points:

  • the same API and data models to read city data (interoperability level 1);
  • the same way to share data under control, between organisations that do not have to trust each other in advance (level 2: data spaces).

A service built on those points runs in any city that follows them. The MIAIS shows how.

docs.title: The minimal package for TEF nodes
docs.text:
CitCom has two kinds of offer, for different audiences:

  • The TEF nodes offer services to AI and robotics innovators: test sites, data, expertise and assessment. The CitCom TEF website lists them.
  • CitCom's work package 3 (WP3) offers the TEF nodes a minimal package: a common reference architecture, with the guides, tools and deployment examples to apply it. Nodes that adopt it share a common technical base, so a service built on that base can run in any of them. This hub gathers the package:
