docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Build on the CitCom data space. Start with a worked example: the MIAIS shows an AI service that goes from a custom integration to a data space service, and Valencia shows a city that offers its existing platform as a data provider. Then follow the guides: each one covers one task, from start to finish, in the CitCom data space. They all follow the same structure: what you will get, what you need, the steps, how to check that it works and what to do if it does not.

Guide For You end up with Join the data space The legal representative (LEAR) of an organisation Your organisation registered and trusted, able to buy in the marketplace Deploy your own connector Operators A consumer connector that issues your organisation's credentials Get a wallet and your credentials Anyone A wallet with your credential, ready to log in Use data from your code Developers of a consumer A program that reads another organisation's data Publish a dataset Data providers An offer in the marketplace that others can buy Publish a web service Service providers A web app that people from other organisations open with their wallet

To read data as soon as possible

Follow Join the data space, then Use data from your code. The first one tells you whether you need your own connector.

flowchart LR
    D["Deploy a connector<br/>(optional)"] -.-> J["Join"]
    J --> W["Get a wallet"]
    W --> C["Use data"]
    W --> P["Publish a dataset"]
    W --> S["Publish a service"]

New to data spaces?

Read Data spaces in 5 minutes first. The guides use its vocabulary: participant, connector, credential, offer and policy.

docs.title: Use data from your code
docs.text:
What you will get: a Python program that reads the data of another organisation through its connector, with a MachineCredential of your organisation. It works the same for any data offer in the marketplace.

flowchart LR
    subgraph YOU["Your organisation"]
        P["Your program<br/>ds-consumer-auth + FiLiP"]
        KC["Your credential issuer<br/>Keycloak"]
    end
    subgraph PROV["The provider's connector"]
        VF["Verifier"]
        GW["Gateway<br/>NGSI-LD API"]
    end
    P -- "1 · MachineCredential" --> KC
    P -- "2 · credential → access token" --> VF
    P -- "3 · NGSI-LD queries + token" --> GW

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Your organisation registered in the data space, with your own connector: it issues the MachineCredential of your programs. The realm created by the onboarding portal does not issue it yet.
  • Its legal representative (LEAR) able to log in to the marketplace.
  • Access to the admin console of your Keycloak, to create a machine user.
  • Python 3.10 or later.

docs.title: 1. Choose an offer and note its access details
docs.text:
Open the marketplace, find the dataset and open its offer. The description of every data offer gives what your program needs:

Detail Where Example API address of the provider API access https://apisix-<provider>.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu and a path such as /ngsi-ld Entity type API access, Available data WasteContainer Verifier of the provider and scope Access https://verifier-<provider>.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/services/machine-id, scope operator1 Role your credential must carry The offer's credential policy clearence1

To try it: the Valencia offers

The Ajuntament de València offers four datasets that are always on. They are a good first test; the rest of this guide uses its Waste containers offer as the example. Replace the values with those of your offer.

docs.title: 2. Create a machine user in your Keycloak
docs.text:
Your program logs in as a user of its own, never as a person. In the admin console of your Keycloak:

  1. Users → Add user: a name such as reader1, with an email. Then Credentials → Set password, not temporary.
  2. Role mapping → Assign role → Filter by clients: choose the role the offer asks for in the client roles-dataspace (clearence1). Give it only the roles of the offers this program uses: the provider's verifier rejects a credential that carries a role the purchase does not allow.
  3. Bind the MachineCredential to the user. See Create the users: having the role is not enough.

docs.title: 3. Buy the offer
docs.text: The LEAR logs in to the marketplace, opens the offer and buys it. When the order is completed, the provider's connector trusts the MachineCredential of your organisation and loads the access policy of the offer. This takes a few seconds.

docs.title: 4. Install the libraries
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install "ds-consumer-auth @ git+https://github.com/CitComAI-Hub/ds-consumer-auth@v0.1.0" filip

ds-consumer-auth gets the credential and the access token, and renews them. FiLiP is the NGSI-LD client.

docs.title: 5. Configure
docs.text:
.env
# Your organisation: who you are
export DS_ISSUER_URL="https://<your Keycloak host>/realms/<your realm>"
export DS_USERNAME="reader1"
export DS_PASSWORD="<its password>"
# The provider: who you ask (from step 1)
export DS_VERIFIER_URL="https://verifier-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/services/machine-id"
export DS_SCOPE="operator1"

source .env

Keep the password out of your repository.

docs.title: 6. Check the token
docs.text:
ds-token > /dev/null && echo "token OK"

If it prints token OK, your credential is accepted by the provider. If not, see If something fails before going on.

docs.title: 7. Read the data
docs.text:
read_data.py
from filip.clients.ngsi_ld.cb import ContextBrokerLDClient
from filip.models.base import FiwareLDHeader
from ds_consumer_auth import data_space_session

cb = ContextBrokerLDClient(
    # API address + path, without /ngsi-ld (FiLiP adds it)
    url="https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/lepus",
    session=data_space_session(),  # adds the data space token to every request
    fiware_header=FiwareLDHeader(),
    create_tenant=False,
)
for entity in cb.get_entity_list(entity_type="WasteContainer", limit=10):
    print(entity.id, entity.model_dump().get("fillingLevel"))

python read_data.py

It prints ten entities. To read more, page with offset, or filter with q, for example q="fillingLevel>0.8".

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
The same query with curl, using the token of the library:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(ds-token)" -H "Accept: application/ld+json" \
  "https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/lepus/ngsi-ld/v1/entities?type=WasteContainer&limit=1"

It returns one entity in JSON-LD.

docs.title: Several offers
docs.text:
• Same provider, same role: one machine user and one session are enough. Each purchase adds the access policy of its offer.
  • Offers that ask for different roles: use one machine user per role. A credential is accepted only if all its roles are allowed by one purchase, so a user with two roles fails both.
  • Several providers: one session per provider, each with the verifier of its provider:
from ds_consumer_auth import ConsumerConfig, data_space_session

def session_for(provider_verifier: str):
    return data_space_session(ConsumerConfig(
        issuer_url="https://<your Keycloak host>/realms/<your realm>",
        username="reader1",
        password="<its password>",
        verifier_url=provider_verifier,
        scope="operator1",
    ))

docs.title: If something fails
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix login: request failed (HTTP 401) Wrong user or password, or DS_ISSUER_URL points to another realm Check them in your Keycloak The credential request fails, or the account console says You have no verifiable credentials yet The MachineCredential is not bound to the machine user Step 2.3 vp_token: the verifier rejected the credential (HTTP 400: {}) The provider does not trust your organisation for MachineCredential: the offer is not bought, or the order is not completed. Or the machine user has a role the offer does not allow Check the order in the marketplace; leave only the offer's role on the machine user The same 400, and the order is completed Your organisation is not in the trust anchor, or the provider cannot resolve your DID Check that your registration is approved and that your did.json is reachable from the internet 401 from the provider's gateway A token from another verifier, or the wrong scope Check DS_VERIFIER_URL and DS_SCOPE 403 from the provider's gateway The token is valid, but no purchased policy allows this request Check that the path and the entity type are those of the offer you bought The query returns [] The access is fine, but there is no entity of that type in that path Check the entity type and the path in the offer

docs.title: Deploy your own connector
docs.text:
What you will get: a consumer connector for your organisation in your own Kubernetes cluster. It gives your organisation a DID and issues its credentials: the LegalPersonCredential of its legal representative, to buy in the marketplace, and the MachineCredential of its programs, to read data. That is all a consumer needs; the provider components can be added later.

First version of this guide

The configuration comes from the connectors running in the CitCom data space, but this guide has not yet been followed from start to finish on a new cluster. Report anything that does not work in the repository.

flowchart LR
    subgraph NS["Your namespace"]
        KC["Keycloak<br/>issues the credentials"]
        DH["did-helper<br/>publishes did.json"]
        PG[("PostgreSQL")]
        KEY["DID key<br/>Secret"]
        KC --- PG
        KEY --> KC
        KEY --> DH
    end
    W["Wallet of the LEAR"] -- "LegalPersonCredential" --> KC
    P["Your programs"] -- "MachineCredential" --> KC
    V["Verifiers of the data space"] -- "resolve your DID" --> DH

The same key signs your credentials (in Keycloak) and is published in your DID document (by did-helper). That is how the verifiers of other participants check that a credential is yours.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster reachable from the internet, with an ingress controller (ingress-nginx).
  • cert-manager with two ClusterIssuers: one for Let's Encrypt (here letsencrypt) and one self-signed (here selfsigned-issuer).
  • Two public host names in a domain you control, pointing to your ingress. This guide uses:
    • did.example.org: your DID will be did:web:did.example.org;
    • keycloak.example.org: your credential issuer.
  • kubectl and Helm 3.

Replace example.org with your domain everywhere.

docs.title: 1. Create the namespace and the secrets
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace connector

# Admin password of Keycloak, and the password of the keystore that holds the DID key
kubectl -n connector create secret generic issuance-secret \
  --from-literal=keycloak-admin="$(openssl rand -base64 24)" \
  --from-literal=store-pass="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"

# Database user of Keycloak
kubectl -n connector create secret generic database-credentials \
  --from-literal=username=keycloak \
  --from-literal=password="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"

docs.title: 2. Create the DID key
docs.text:
An EC P-256 key, issued by the self-signed issuer. Its certificate is only a container for the key: it is not used for TLS.

did-key.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: did-key
  namespace: connector
spec:
  commonName: did.example.org
  dnsNames: [did.example.org]
  secretName: did-key
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
  usages: [digital signature, key encipherment]
  issuerRef:
    group: cert-manager.io
    kind: ClusterIssuer
    name: selfsigned-issuer

kubectl apply -f did-key.yaml
kubectl -n connector wait --for=condition=Ready certificate/did-key --timeout=120s

docs.title: 3. Publish your DID with did-helper
docs.text:
did-helper.yaml
image:
  repository: quay.io/seamware/did-helper
  tag: 0.4.4
config:
  server:
    hostUrl: https://did.example.org
    certPath: /certs/tls.crt
  generateKey:
    enabled: false
volumes:
  - name: certs
    secret:
      secretName: did-key
      items: [{ key: tls.crt, path: tls.crt }]
volumeMounts:
  - { name: certs, mountPath: /certs, readOnly: true }
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
  hosts:
    - host: did.example.org
      paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }]
  tls:
    - secretName: did-example-org-tls
      hosts: [did.example.org]

helm repo add fiware https://fiware.github.io/helm-charts/
helm install did fiware/did-helper -n connector -f did-helper.yaml

Check it, from a machine outside your network:

curl -s https://did.example.org/.well-known/did.json

It returns a DID document whose id is did:web:did.example.org.

docs.title: 4. Install PostgreSQL and Keycloak
docs.text:
PostgreSQL, with a database for Keycloak:

postgres.yaml
fullnameOverride: postgres
auth:
  username: keycloak
  database: keycloak
  existingSecret: database-credentials
  secretKeys:
    adminPasswordKey: password

helm install postgres oci://registry-1.docker.io/cloudpirates/postgres --version 0.20.3 \
  -n connector -f postgres.yaml

The realm. Download the consumer realm and replace the two host names:

curl -sLO https://citcomai-hub.github.io/assets/connector/consumer-realm.json
sed -i 's/DID_HOST/did.example.org/g; s/KEYCLOAK_HOST/keycloak.example.org/g' consumer-realm.json
kubectl -n connector create configmap realm --from-file=provider-realm.json=consumer-realm.json

The realm, called provider, defines everything the data space expects from an issuer:

Item Value Used by Credential LegalPersonCredential SD-JWT (dc+sd-jwt), ES256, bound to the holder's key; claims firstName, lastName, email, and roles from the client marketplace The marketplace login Credential MachineCredential Same format; claims email and roles from the client roles-dataspace The verifiers of the providers Credential ServiceCredential Same format; claims from roles-dataspace Web services bought by your organisation Client marketplace Role REPRESENTATIVE The LEAR Client roles-dataspace Roles clearence1 to clearence4; add the roles your offers ask for Your programs and people Client account-console Direct access grants and OID4VCI enabled ds-consumer-auth and the wallets Signing key The DID key, from the keystore /did-material/cert.pfx, with kid = your DID Every credential

The ${…} values left in the file (${STORE_PASS}, ${role_…}) are read by Keycloak itself: leave them as they are.

Keycloak. It must be the SEAMWARE image 26.6.2: it includes the credential offer endpoint that the wallets and ds-consumer-auth use. An init container packs the DID key into the keystore that the realm reads.

keycloak.yaml
image:
  registry: quay.io
  repository: seamware/keycloak
  tag: "26.6.2"
keycloak:
  adminUser: keycloak-admin
  existingSecret: issuance-secret
  secretKeys:
    adminPasswordKey: keycloak-admin
  hostname: https://keycloak.example.org
  httpEnabled: true
  httpsEnabled: false   # TLS ends at the ingress
  proxyHeaders: xforwarded
  production: true
# Keep the providers and themes bundled in the SEAMWARE image
preserveProviders: true
preserveThemes: true
extraEnvVars:
  - name: STORE_PASS
    valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: issuance-secret, key: store-pass } }
extraVolumes:
  - { name: did-material, emptyDir: {} }
  - { name: realms, configMap: { name: realm } }
  - { name: did-key, secret: { secretName: did-key } }
extraVolumeMounts:
  - { name: did-material, mountPath: /did-material }
  - { name: realms, mountPath: /opt/keycloak/data/import }
extraInitContainers:
  - name: create-did-keystore
    image: ubuntu:22.04
    command: [/bin/bash, -ec]
    args:
      - |
        apt-get -y update && apt-get -y install --no-install-recommends openssl ca-certificates
        openssl pkcs12 -export -out /did-material/cert.pfx \
          -inkey /did-key/tls.key -in /did-key/tls.crt \
          -certfile /etc/ssl/certs/ISRG_Root_X1.pem \
          -name didPrivateKey -passout env:STORE_PASS
        chmod 666 /did-material/cert.pfx
    env:
      - name: STORE_PASS
        valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: issuance-secret, key: store-pass } }
    volumeMounts:
      - { name: did-material, mountPath: /did-material }
      - { name: did-key, mountPath: /did-key }
realm:
  import: true
features:
  enabled: [oid4vc-vci, oid4vc-vci-preauth-code, oid4vc-vci-rest-credential-offer]
postgres:
  enabled: false
database:
  type: postgres
  host: postgres
  port: "5432"
  name: keycloak
  existingSecret: database-credentials
  secretKeys: { usernameKey: username, passwordKey: password }
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
  hosts:
    - host: keycloak.example.org
      paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }]
  tls:
    - secretName: keycloak-example-org-tls
      hosts: [keycloak.example.org]
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 640Mi }
  limits: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi }

helm install keycloak oci://registry-1.docker.io/cloudpirates/keycloak --version 0.21.4 \
  -n connector -f keycloak.yaml
kubectl -n connector rollout status statefulset/keycloak --timeout=10m

Check that it issues credentials:

curl -s https://keycloak.example.org/realms/provider/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(sorted(json.load(sys.stdin)["credential_configurations_supported"]))'

It prints ['LegalPersonCredential', 'MachineCredential', 'ServiceCredential'].

The realm is imported only once

Keycloak imports the realm file only if the realm does not exist yet. Later changes to the file do not reach a running Keycloak: make them in the admin console, or with its admin API.

docs.title: 5. Create the users
docs.text:
Open the admin console at https://keycloak.example.org/admin, user keycloak-admin, with the password of step 1:

kubectl -n connector get secret issuance-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.keycloak-admin}' | base64 -d; echo

In the realm provider, create one user per role, never one user for everything:

User Roles (client → role) Credential to bind The LEAR, with email, first and last name marketplace → REPRESENTATIVE LegalPersonCredential A machine user for each program, such as reader1 roles-dataspace → the role of the offers it reads (clearence1) MachineCredential

For each one: Users → Add user, then Credentials → Set password (not temporary), then Role mapping → Assign role.

Having the role is not enough: Keycloak only issues the credentials that are bound to the user. Bind them with the admin API:

KC=https://keycloak.example.org
ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(kubectl -n connector get secret issuance-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.keycloak-admin}' | base64 -d)
TOKEN=$(curl -s "$KC/realms/master/protocol/openid-connect/token" \
  -d grant_type=password -d client_id=admin-cli -d username=keycloak-admin \
  --data-urlencode "password=$ADMIN_PASSWORD" | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["access_token"])')

bind() {  # bind <username> <credential>
  USER_ID=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$KC/admin/realms/provider/users?username=$1&exact=true" \
    | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["id"])')
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$1 $2: %{http_code}\n" -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"credentialScopeName\": \"$2\"}" \
    "$KC/admin/realms/provider/users/$USER_ID/vc/credentials"
}
bind lear LegalPersonCredential
bind reader1 MachineCredential

Each call prints a 2xx code. Log in to the account console ($KC/realms/provider/account) as each user: Verifiable Credentials lists the bound credential.

docs.title: 6. Register in the data space
docs.text: Join the data space with option B and your DID, did:web:did.example.org. When the registration is approved, your credentials are trusted.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
With the machine user, the ds-consumer-auth library can get a credential from your Keycloak:

pip install "ds-consumer-auth @ git+https://github.com/CitComAI-Hub/ds-consumer-auth@v0.1.0"
python3 - <<'EOF'
from ds_consumer_auth import ConsumerConfig, CredentialIssuer, HolderKey
issuer = CredentialIssuer(ConsumerConfig(
    issuer_url="https://keycloak.example.org/realms/provider",
    username="reader1", password="<its password>"))
credential = issuer.issue(HolderKey.generate())
print(credential.claims["iss"], credential.claims["vct"])
EOF

It prints did:web:did.example.org MachineCredential. To read data, buy an offer and follow Use data from your code.

docs.title: Before going to production
docs.text:
• Back up the Secret did-key: if the key is lost, your organisation needs a new DID and a new registration.
  • Keep the Keycloak admin password and the user passwords in a secret store, not in a repository.
  • Give each user and program only the roles it needs. A verifier rejects a credential that carries a role the purchase does not allow.

docs.title: If something fails
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix did.json returns 404 or a TLS error The ingress or the Let's Encrypt certificate of did.example.org is not ready kubectl -n connector get ingress,certificate The credential endpoints fail, or Keycloak logs errors about missing OID4VC providers The chart hid the providers of the image Keep preserveProviders: true Keycloak does not start: keystore error STORE_PASS differs between the init container and Keycloak, or the key Secret is missing Both read issuance-secret; check that did-key exists The issuer metadata does not list the credentials Wrong image, or the OID4VCI features are not enabled Use quay.io/seamware/keycloak:26.6.2 and the three features of step 4 The metadata shows http:// addresses Keycloak does not see the original scheme Keep hostname: https://… and proxyHeaders: xforwarded You have no verifiable credentials yet in the account console The credential is not bound to the user The bind call of step 5 The verifiers of other participants reject your credentials Your registration is not approved, or the kid of the key does not match your DID Check the status in the onboarding portal; check that DID_HOST was replaced in the realm

docs.title: Become a provider
docs.text:
To publish data or services, the connector also needs the provider components of the FIWARE Data Space Connector (CitCom runs version 10):

Component Role Verifier Turns the credentials of other organisations into access tokens APISIX + OPA Gateway in front of your data and services, with the policy engine ODRL-PAP and Trusted Issuers List Your access policies and the organisations you trust contract-management Applies the purchases of your offers coming from the marketplace An NGSI-LD broker Your data, or Lepus in front of an NGSI-v2 platform

See Inside a connector for how they work together, then Publish a dataset. Lessons from running them in CitCom:

  • Extra routes: the chart's default route /ngsi-ld/* goes to its built-in broker. Routes for other brokers (such as /lepus/ngsi-ld/*) or web services are added to APISIX with the same token check and OPA policy.
  • contract-management must be reachable by the marketplace; set its address in your organisation's marketplace profile.
  • Images: deploy your own images with a new version tag each time; a node does not pull again a tag it already has.

docs.title: Learn locally first
docs.text:
• The CitCom Minimum Viable Data Space deploys a minimal FIWARE data space (trust anchor, provider and consumer) in a local Kind cluster.
  • FIWARE's local deployment is more complete and needs more resources.

docs.title: Join the data space
docs.text: What you will get: your organisation registered in the CitCom FIWARE data space. The other participants trust the credentials it issues, and its legal representative can log in to the marketplace to buy offers.

docs.title: Two ways to get your organisation's identity
docs.text:
Your organisation needs a credential issuer: the service that issues the credentials of its people and programs. The legal representative logs in to the marketplace with a LegalPersonCredential, and your programs read data with a MachineCredential.

A. The portal creates it B. Your own connector What you deploy Nothing A consumer connector: Keycloak and did-helper Your identity A realm of your own in the Keycloak of the onboarding portal, with a new DID Your connector's DID, on your domain Who manages your users You, in the admin console of your realm You, in your Keycloak Log in to the marketplace and buy Yes Yes Your programs read the data you bought Not yet Yes Best for Starting now, and exploring and buying in the marketplace Reading data from code, running your own infrastructure, or becoming a provider

Start with A if you want to be in the data space today. With B, deploy your connector first: you register with its DID.

Reading data with option A

Today the realm created by the portal issues the credential of the legal representative, not the MachineCredential that programs need to read data. To read data from code now, use option B.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The legal representative (LEAR) of the organisation, who acts for it and signs the participation agreement, with an email address.
  • With option B: the DID of your connector, for example did:web:did.example.org, with its document reachable at https://did.example.org/.well-known/did.json.

docs.title: 1. Fill in the registration form
docs.text: Open the onboarding portal and start a new registration. Fill in the legal data of the organisation and the contact of its representative.

docs.title: 2. Digital identity
docs.text:
In the Digital identity section of the form:

  • Option A: leave the did:web field empty. The portal will create your identity when the registration is approved.
  • Option B: enter the DID of your connector.

docs.title: 3. Sign the participation agreement
docs.text: Download the participation agreement from the form, have the LEAR sign it, and upload the signed copy. Submit the registration.

docs.title: 4. Wait for the approval
docs.text:
The data space operator reviews the request. When it approves it, the portal registers your organisation in the trust anchor automatically. From that moment the credentials your organisation issues are trusted in the data space. You can follow the status of the request in the portal.

With option A, the approval also creates your realm in the Keycloak of the onboarding portal, with your new DID (did:web:onboarding.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu:<your realm>). You receive an email with a link to set the password of its administrator, the user admin, and the address of its admin console: https://keycloak-onboarding.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/admin/<your realm>/console/.

docs.title: 5. Create the user of the legal representative
docs.text:
In the admin console of your Keycloak (the realm created by the portal with option A, your own one with option B):

  1. Create a user for the LEAR, with email, first name and last name, and set its password.
  2. Let it receive the LegalPersonCredential:
    • Option A: nothing to do. Every new user of the realm joins the group representative, which lets it log in to the marketplace.
    • Option B: follow Create the users of the connector guide.

With option B, create the users for your programs later, when you need them: see Use data from your code.

docs.title: 6. Get the credential and log in to the marketplace
docs.text: Follow Get a wallet and your credentials to put the LegalPersonCredential in the LEAR's wallet. Then open the marketplace, click Log in and scan the QR code with the wallet. The first login creates your organisation in the marketplace.

docs.title: 7. Complete the profile
docs.text: In the marketplace, complete the profile of your organisation: trading name, website, country and a short description, in English.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
• After logging in, the marketplace shows the name of your organisation.
  • The LEAR can open any offer and sees the button to buy it.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• To read data from your code: Use data from your code.
  • To offer your own data later, you need your own connector with the provider components: see Become a provider.

docs.title: If something fails
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The marketplace rejects the LEAR's login The registration is not approved yet, or the credential is not a LegalPersonCredential of your organisation Check the status in the portal and the credential in the wallet A registration with your own DID is not approved The operator cannot resolve your DID Open https://<your DID host>/.well-known/did.json from outside your network: it must return your DID document You have no verifiable credentials yet in the account console The credential is not assigned to the user Repeat step 5 for that user No email after the approval (option A) The message went to spam, or the address in the form is wrong Check the spam folder; otherwise contact the operator through the portal The marketplace home is empty and the browser console shows 401 on /catalog/… An expired session in the browser Log out, or delete the marketplace cookies

docs.title: Publish a dataset
docs.text: What you will get: a dataset of your organisation offered in the marketplace. Whoever buys it can read it through your connector, and only it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Your organisation registered, with its own connector and the contract management address in its marketplace profile.
  • The data in an NGSI-LD broker behind your connector, described with Smart Data Models:
    • a broker of your own (Orion-LD, Scorpio), loaded by your ingestion process; or
    • your existing NGSI-v2 platform, served as NGSI-LD by Lepus, as the Ajuntament de València does.
  • A route in your connector's gateway (APISIX) to that broker, protected by the verifier token and the policy engine (OPA), as the default /ngsi-ld/* route is.

docs.title: 1. Decide what the offer grants
docs.text:
One offer per dataset keeps things simple. For each one, write down:

  • the path of its route, e.g. /ngsi-ld or /lepus/ngsi-ld;
  • its entity type, e.g. WasteContainer;
  • the credential and role that buyers will present: MachineCredential and a role such as clearence1.

docs.title: 2. Write the two characteristics
docs.text:
An offer carries two characteristics that your connector applies on every purchase:

Verifier policyODRL policy

Which credentials the verifier accepts from the buyer (credentialsConfiguration): the credential type and the allowed values of the data space roles.

{
  "credentialsType": "MachineCredential",
  "claims": [{
    "name": "roles",
    "path": "$.roles[?(@.target==\"roles-dataspace\")].names[*]",
    "allowedValues": ["clearence1"]
  }]
}

What the buyer can do (authorizationPolicy): here, use the WasteContainer entities under /lepus/ngsi-ld, with a MachineCredential that has the role clearence1.

{
  "@type": "odrl:Policy",
  "odrl:uid": "https://<participant>.<domain>/policy/waste-containers-access",
  "odrl:permission": [{
    "odrl:assigner": "did:web:<participant>.<domain>",
    "odrl:action": "odrl:use",
    "odrl:target": {
      "@type": "odrl:AssetCollection",
      "odrl:source": "urn:asset",
      "odrl:refinement": {
        "@type": "odrl:LogicalConstraint",
        "odrl:and": [
          {"odrl:leftOperand": "http:path", "odrl:operator": "http:isInPath",
           "odrl:rightOperand": "/lepus/ngsi-ld"},
          {"odrl:leftOperand": "ngsi-ld:entityType", "odrl:operator": "odrl:eq",
           "odrl:rightOperand": "WasteContainer"}
        ]
      }
    },
    "odrl:assignee": {
      "@type": "odrl:PartyCollection",
      "odrl:source": "urn:user",
      "odrl:refinement": {
        "@type": "odrl:LogicalConstraint",
        "odrl:and": [
          {"odrl:leftOperand": "vc:role", "odrl:operator": "odrl:hasPart",
           "odrl:rightOperand": "clearence1"},
          {"odrl:leftOperand": "vc:type", "odrl:operator": "odrl:hasPart",
           "odrl:rightOperand": "MachineCredential"}
        ]
      }
    }
  }]
}

The full version, with the @context and typed values, is in the Valencia offers used as reference.

docs.title: 3. Create the offer in the marketplace
docs.text:
Log in to the marketplace with the LEAR's wallet, and in My offerings:

  1. Create a catalogue for your organisation, if you do not have one.
  2. Create the product specification: name, description, terms of use, an image (it is required to show the offer on the home page) and the two characteristics above.
  3. Create the product offering in your catalogue, with a category and a price (free is fine), and launch it.

Write all texts in English: CitCom is international.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text: Buy the offer from a test organisation, then read the data as in Use data from your code. Also check what must fail: another entity type returns 403, and an organisation that did not buy returns an error at the verifier.

docs.title: If something fails
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The purchase completes but nothing changes in your connector The contract management address is missing in your profile, or a characteristic was saved without its value type Fix the profile; recreate the characteristics with credentialsConfiguration and authorizationPolicy value types The buyer gets 403 for the right path and type The policy was not loaded in the policy engine Check the policy; if you load one by hand, use an id without hyphens: hyphenated ids are accepted but never applied The buyer's credential is rejected even though they bought Their credential carries a role that the offer does not allow All the data space roles of a credential must be allowed by the purchase: give machine users only the data role The offer does not appear on the marketplace home The specification has no image Add a Profile Picture attachment

docs.title: Publish a web service
docs.text: What you will get: a web application offered in the marketplace. People from the organisations that buy it open it with their wallet; you write no login code. The MIAIS is published this way.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Your organisation registered, with its own connector.
  • The web application deployed next to the connector, reachable by its gateway (APISIX) but not published directly.
  • The application must work under a path prefix (for example /waste-collection/): use relative URLs in its pages and calls.

docs.title: 1. Choose a role for the service
docs.text: Create a role for the service in your Keycloak, in the client of the data space roles (roles-dataspace), for example waste_collection_user. This role goes into the ServiceCredential of the people who use the service. Every organisation that buys the service creates the same role in its own Keycloak and gives it only to the people who will use it.

docs.title: 2. Put the application behind the gateway
docs.text:
Add a route to your APISIX for the prefix, /waste-collection/*, with:

  • the openid-connect plugin with bearer_only: false, pointing to your verifier's service-id service: a visitor without a session is sent to the verifier's QR login, and after it, APISIX keeps an encrypted session cookie;
  • the opa plugin, so the policy engine checks the token on every request, as on the data routes.

Point the public host name of the service to your APISIX, and redirect / to the prefix.

docs.title: 3. Create the offer
docs.text:
As in Publish a dataset, with:

  • the verifier policy for ServiceCredential and your role (allowedValues: ["waste_collection_user"]);
  • an ODRL policy for the path /waste-collection, with vc:type ServiceCredential and vc:role your role;
  • the category AI services, and a screenshot as the image.

The policy works by path, not by host name: that is why the service lives under its own prefix, and why the policy does not give access to anything else in your gateway.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
1. A test organisation buys the service and gives the role to a test user, with the ServiceCredential bound to that user.
  2. The test user puts the credential in a wallet, opens the service URL, scans the QR code and shares the credential.
  3. The service opens. A user of an organisation that did not buy it is rejected at the QR login.

docs.title: If something fails
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The login loops or the app loads without styles The app uses absolute URLs Use relative URLs so everything stays under the prefix The verifier rejects a user of a buying organisation The user's credential carries more data space roles than the purchase allows Give the user only the service role You have no verifiable credentials yet for the user The ServiceCredential is not bound to the user Bind the credential to the user in Keycloak, not only the role 403 after a successful login The ODRL policy does not match the path or the role Check the path prefix and the role in the policy

docs.title: Get a wallet and your credentials
docs.text: What you will get: a wallet with a verifiable credential of your organisation, to log in to the marketplace or to a service of the data space by scanning a QR code.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A user in the credential issuer (Keycloak) of your organisation, with the credential bound to it. Your organisation's administrator creates it: see Join the data space.
  • One of these wallets:
Phone: Lissi ID WalletDesktop: atesta-id-wallet

Lissi ID Wallet, from the Play Store. Scan the QR codes with the phone.

atesta-id-wallet, a desktop wallet for Linux and Windows made in CitCom. Download it from its releases page. It reads the QR codes from a screenshot, so you never need a phone. It is a prototype: it uses the EUDI protocols, but it is not a certified EUDI Wallet.

The Wallets page of the toolbox compares both wallets and lists the limitations of atesta-id-wallet.

docs.title: Which credential
docs.text:
Credential You need it to Who gives it to you LegalPersonCredential Act for your organisation in the marketplace: profile, offers, purchases Your organisation, if you are its legal representative (LEAR) ServiceCredential Use a web service bought by your organisation, such as the MIAIS Your organisation, with the role that the service asks for

Programs do not use a wallet: they request a MachineCredential by themselves. See Use data from your code.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the account console of your organisation's Keycloak and log in with your user:
    • Your own connector: https://<your Keycloak host>/realms/provider/account.
    • Identity created by the onboarding portal: the account console of your realm, https://keycloak-onboarding.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/realms/<your realm>/account.
  2. Go to Verifiable Credentials and choose the credential.
  3. Click Issue to wallet. A QR code (or a link) appears.
  4. Scan it with the wallet:
    • Lissi: scan the QR with the phone.
    • atesta-id-wallet: click the link, or press Scan QR and take a screenshot of the QR code.
  5. The wallet shows who issues which credential. Accept, and enter your Keycloak user and password when the wallet asks for them.
  6. The credential appears in the wallet.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text: Open the marketplace and click Log in. Scan the QR code with the wallet. It shows what will be shared; press Share. The browser logs you in.

docs.title: If something fails
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix You have no verifiable credentials yet in the account console The credential is not bound to your user. Having the role is not enough Ask your administrator to bind it (see Create the users) The wallet rejects the offer, or the QR has expired Offers are short-lived Click Issue to wallet again The verifier rejects the login Your organisation is not trusted for this credential, or your roles do not match For the marketplace, your organisation must be registered. For a service, it must have bought it, and you must have only the role it asks for A service rejects a credential that has several roles The verifier requires every data space role in the credential to be allowed by the purchase Use a user with only the role of that service

docs.title: Local Digital Twins
docs.text: Local Digital Twins (LDTs) are at the forefront of transforming how cities and communities leverage data and technology to address complex challenges.

docs.title: Towards AI-ready & interoperable LDTs
docs.text: As the demand for AI-ready and interoperable systems grows, it becomes imperative to establish a unified approach that ensures seamless integration and collaboration across diverse LDT environments. This section introduces the collective efforts and strategic vision aimed at achieving this goal, setting the stage for the technical and strategic objectives outlined below. By fostering interoperability and aligning with open standards, we pave the way for scalable, sustainable, and innovative solutions that benefit both local and European-wide initiatives.

docs.title: Strategic Goals
docs.text:
• Assess Cross-Site Interoperability: Evaluate the feasibility and value of enhancing interoperability among LDTs across TEF sites
  • Evolve LDTs: Recommend improvements to LDTs and explore common cross-site infrastructure (e.g., data spaces, AI model repositories)
  • Define Joint Pilots: Identify and test pilots to validate proposed ideas in real-world scenarios

docs.title: Technical Goals
docs.text:
• Aligning with the EU LDT Toolbox, FIWARE and open standards like ETSI NGSI-LD
  • Ensuring LDTs can seamlessly integrate AI models by providing structured, standardized, and accessible data
  • Develop a “blueprint” for interoperable LDTs across TEF sites
  • Identifying and standardizing thematic datasets to enable seamless cross-site data exchange
  • Applying MIMs and best practices to ensure scalability and sustainability.

To facilitate collaboration and drive progress towards these goals, we established the LDT Club—a dedicated forum where stakeholders can share insights, align strategies, and collectively address challenges. This collaborative platform serves as a cornerstone for fostering innovation and ensuring that the transition to AI-ready and interoperable LDTs is both inclusive and effective.

Meeting minutes, recordings and further materials related to the LDT Club are available under https://imecinternational.sharepoint.com/:f:/r/sites/Citcom.aiTEF/Shared%20Documents/WP3%20-%20Infrastructure/T3.2/LDT%20Club?csf=1&web=1&e=zyhvcL.

For more details on the tools and methodologies supporting the development of Local Digital Twins, refer to the LDT Toolkit.

docs.title: Scenario: CitCom.AI – EDIC LDT - CitiVerse
docs.text: The scenario illustrated in the diagram above puts the LDT CitiVerse EDIC and CitCom.AI TEF sites in relation. While the EDIC aims at creating a federated network of Local Digital Twins (LDTs) across Europe, CitCom.AI leverages LDTs to test and integrate AI solutions, fostering innovation in Smart Cities and Communities. AI innovators begin by collaborating with CitCom.AI TEF sites, where they can access real-world LDT environments to develop, test, and validate their AI solutions. Ideally, these environments should provide standardized, interoperable data and infrastructure aligned with EU LDT Toolbox guidelines. Once solutions are successfully demonstrated within CitCom.AI, innovators can leverage the established interoperability and best practices to integrate their solutions into the broader EDIC federated LDT network. This pathway ensures that innovations are not only tested in realistic scenarios but are also ready for seamless adoption and scaling across multiple European cities and communities through the EDIC framework. To ensure interoperability, the CitCom.AI LDTs, currently a set of heterogeneous and independent systems, should adopt common standards and frameworks outlined in the EU LDT Toolbox. This includes aligning data models, APIs, and communication protocols to enable seamless integration and collaboration across the EDIC federated LDT network. Conducting a gap analysis between CitCom.AI LDTs and the EU LDT Toolbox is crucial to identify areas where alignment is needed. This analysis will help pinpoint discrepancies in data models, APIs, and communication protocols, ensuring that AI solutions tested within CitComAI can transition seamlessly to the EDIC federated network. By addressing these gaps, the pathway for AI innovators to scale their solutions across Europe becomes more efficient and less fragmented.

docs.title: How to start with a gap analysis?
docs.text:
The diagram above illustrates the different layers and tools of the EU LDT Toolbox. Each sticky note at the border of the diagram links a question about your existing LDT with the relevant layer of the EU LDT Toolbox. Answering these questions provides a structured starting point for further elaboration of a gap analysis, helping to identify areas where alignment with the toolbox is needed.

Starting from the bottom to the top layer, the following questions help structure your gap analysis. Each question is paired with its rationale and expected outcome to guide your assessment:

docs.title: 1. Question: What are the city-services supported by your LDT?
docs.text: Related layer: Services Why it matters: It clarifies which service domains (e.g. mobility, energy, waste) each LDT addresses. This helps identify overlaps, complementary areas, and opportunities for aligning use-case-specific models or indicators. Outcome: Provides a shared view of functional scope across partners, guiding discussions on domain priorities and potential areas for interoperability or joint development.

docs.title: 2. Question: What data sources do we have and in which formats?
docs.text: Related layer: Data Sources Why it matters: Data heterogeneity is a major barrier to interoperability. Knowing the sources (IoT, legacy systems, GIS, etc.) helps assess compatibility. Outcome: Supports data model alignment, semantic mapping, and standardization efforts across partners.

docs.title: 3. Question: What standards in terms of interoperability are you already supporting?
docs.text: Related layer: Interoperability Layer Why it matters: This directly touches on technical alignment: APIs, data standards (e.g., NGSI-LD, OGC), middleware, ontologies, etc. Outcome: Helps to map the interoperability landscape, uncover gaps, and guide toward converging on shared mechanisms (e.g., FIWARE, IDS, GAIA-X standards).

docs.title: 4. Question: How do you retrieve, store and publish data?
docs.text: Related layer: Data Acquisition Why it matters: Covers the full data lifecycle and reveals differences in how data is made accessible, which impacts interoperability and reuse. Outcome: Identifies common patterns and gaps in data handling to support alignment on shared access and publishing approaches.

docs.title: 5. Question: Elaborate whether you use or plan to use AI in your LDT. If yes, what kind of AI (LLMs, predictive models, classifiers etc.) and for what purpose?
docs.text: Related layer: Knowledge Why it matters: Captures both current capabilities and future intentions, helping assess AI maturity and identify relevant tools, methods, and gaps. Outcome: Maps the AI landscape across LDTs, revealing opportunities for reuse, collaboration, or shared infrastructure for AI integration.

docs.title: 6. Question: What data pipelines are you currently using between the different layers of your LDT?
docs.text: Related layer: Orchestration Why it matters: It clarifies which service domains each LDT targets, helping identify overlaps, complementary focus areas, and opportunities for aligning use-case-specific models or indicators. Outcome: Provides a shared view of functional scope across partners, guiding discussions on domain priorities and potential areas for interoperability or joint development.

docs.title: 7. Question: What kind of visualizations is your LDT supporting?
docs.text: Related layer: Visualization Why it matters: Visualizations are a key interface between the Local Digital Twin (LDT) and its users. Outcome: It gives a clear overview of current visualization capabilities and technologies (Kepler.gl, PowerBI, Grafana etc.).

docs.title: Resulting Examples
docs.text: The following sections provide two examples where the template has been applied.

docs.title: Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology / Luxembourg TEF - LDT For Electromobility​
docs.text:
Question: What are the city-services supported by your LDT? Answer: Our LDT is meant to enable city planners & mobility operators to monitor and optimise EV related infrastructure. It is supposed to empower decision-making through predictive analytics, scenario testing ("What-if scenarios"), and monitoring, fostering greener and smarter urban​ development.

Question: What data sources do we have and in which formats? Anwer: We deal with data about energy consumption and production. The data comes from simulation engines, REST APIs, or historical datasets. The data format is mainly JSON.

Question: What standards in terms of interoperability are you already supporting? Answer: Our architecture is based on custom micro services and Azure components. Communication happens mainly via REST APIs (documented using OpenAPI 3.0) or Azure Event Grid. Since we are relying on Azure DT our digital twin model is based on DTDL v3. For any geospatial data we rely on GeoJSON.

Question How do you retrieve, store and publish data? Answer: Entities and their relationships are stored in a Neo4j graph database, while telemetry data is kept as timeseries in InfluxDB. We also use Minio (S3) as a kind of staging storage. However, this data is not yet published.

Question: Elaborate whether you use or plan to use AI in your LDT. If yes, what kind of AI (LLMs, predictive models, classifiers etc.) and for what purpose? Answer: A user can define scenario/new entities parameters to trigger the generation of synthetic (simulations) or forecasting (deep learning) data. Several purposes: what-if scenarios, forecasting, anomalies detection etc. Results stored in MinIO or InfluxDB and then used for new graphs/entities.

Questions: What data pipelines are you currently using between the different layers of your LDT? Answer: We have various data pipelines that transform e.g. source data into graph entities and telemetry. Those pipelines are YAML declarations, interpreter and executed by RedPanda Connect (formerly benthos). A dedicated micro service allows to us orchestrate such pipelines.

Question: What kind of visualizations is your LDT supporting? Answer: All visualizations are integrated in a single LDT front-end. A mapbox based visualization shows the relevant entities (buildings with PVs, charging stations and POIs) on a geographical map. Chart.js based graphs are built according to city's needs, they can be grouped into a dashboard. Separation of real/historical telemetries and generated one.

docs.title: Aarhus City Lab / Denmark TEF - BIPED Digital Twin​
docs.text:
Question: What are the city-services supported by your LDT? Answer: The BIPED LDT is designed to support city services primarily focused on enabling Positive Energy Districts (PEDs) and enhancing urban sustainability: - PED Planning and Development: The digital twin aims to assist city governments, decision-makers, and local communities in Brabrand/Aarhus in making informed decisions towards PED planning. It provides a holistic view of PED development, encompassing energy, mobility, and cross-sectoral properties. (D1.1 sec 3 and D1.3 sec 3.3) - Climate Goal Acceleration: A core objective is to leverage urban data, including soft data, to accelerate the achievement of local climate goals within Brabrand. (D1.1 sec 6) - Public Participation: The LDT seeks to enhance public participation in achieving positive energy targets by providing access to tools and information. (D1.1 sec 3) - Energy Management: The integration of an "Energy District Heating Load Forecasting Model" indicates support for services related to predicting and managing district heating loads. (D2.2 table 3) - Mobility and Traffic Management: The LDT supports services related to traffic flow and environmental impact analysis through integrated "Macroscopic Traffic Modelling" and its associated energy and environmental impacts modeling. (D2.2 table 3) Besides these defined city-services BiPED also has achieved to promote Open Data and investigated how open data can bring secondary value. Also a hope for BiPED is that it can leverage the agenda for local data management in Aarhus Municipality.

Question: What data sources do we have and in which formats? Answer: BIPED utilizes a variety of data sources in different formats: - Hard and Soft Data: This includes sensor data, IoT data, energy consumption/production data ("hard data"), and information gathered from workshops and citizen engagement activities ("soft data"). (D1.3 sec 3.3) - Environmental Data: Environmental noise measurements are collected at a sensor level in CSV, TXT, and XML formats. Environmental air quality model continuous spatial data is also used. (D1.3 sec 3.3) - Energy Data: Data is obtained from the Center Denmark Energy Platform. (D1.3 sec 3.3) - Mobility Data: Mobility data comes from Road Twin Software. Traffic data is derived from OpenStreetMap and is accessible in a schema compatible with the INSPIRE Transport Network. TomTom Traffic Stats data is also utilized for visualizations. (D1.3 sec 3.3, D2.1 annex 2, D 2.2 table 3) - Geographic and Urban Data: This encompasses geographic data, building data, sensor data, and IoT data. Open Data from the Aarhus open data portal is a source, as are INSPIRE Geoportal Priority Datasets. (D1.3 sec 3.3, D2.1 annex 2) - Energy and weather data: Energy consumptions and local weather data from Kredsløb. Weather forecasts and observations from the Danish meteorological Institute. Historical weather forecasts from the Norwegian meteorological institute.

Full list: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1dpK9yo6ZPDXqMnP3U0ce4DHcQ6XJq2AIpIWSks4Uk38/edit?gid=185146452#gid=185146452

Question: What standards in terms of interoperability are you already supporting? Answer: BIPED places a strong emphasis on interoperability to ensure scalable and sustainable solutions: - Minimum Interoperability Standards (MIMs): The project aims to foster an open technical and policy environment by supporting MIMs to drive and scale sustainable change (D1.1 sec 3 and D1.3 sec 4). - Open Standards: The DKSR OUP, which forms the technical core of the digital twin, is built upon common data models and open standards, including (D1.3 sec 3.6): - OGC API Standards. - IS O/IEC standards. - IT U-T standards. - W3C standards. - DCAT-AP - OGC API Processes: There is a general agreement on using the OGC API Processes standard, which provides guidelines for designing model APIs. This has facilitated the integration of models, such as the Traffic Model from Road Twin. (D2.1 sec 3.4) - OpenAPI Compliance: The DKSR Model Coordinator API is described as OpenAPI compliant, ensuring standardized interaction with integrated models (REST APIs) - Communication Protocols: The digital twin utilizes widely recognized communication protocols like AMQP, MQTT, and REST, which are key for interoperable data exchange between different components and systems. (D1.3 sec 3.4 and D2.1 sec 3.2) - INSPIRE Compatibility: Traffic data is made accessible in a schema compatible with the INSPIRE Transport Network, further ensuring interoperability within a broader European framework. (D2.1 annex 2)

Question: Elaborate whether you use or plan to use AI in your LDT. If yes, what kind of AI (LLMs, predictive models, classifiers etc.) and for what purpose? Answer: Yes, BIPED explicitly plans to use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in its Local Digital Twin (LDT). The project envisions "Future-Ready Intelligent Twins" that will leverage AI to: - Learn and make real-time accurate insights and predictions. - Accurately align real-time operational decisions with longer-term policy. BiPED considers the definition of AI as stated in the AI Watch – determining Artificial Intelligence 2.0 by the European Comission. While specific types of AI like LLMs or classifiers are not explicitly detailed, the focus on "predictions" strongly indicates the use of predictive models. Forecast models are the primary AI models in BiPED currently. The project also considers AI from a regulatory perspective, referencing the "AI Act" in its Data Management Plan, suggesting a structured approach to AI integration.

Question: What data pipelines are you currently using between the different layers of your LDT? Answer: The BIPED Digital Twin's architecture involves several components that interact to form data pipelines: - Architectural Components: The system is composed of back-end components, including the DKSR OUP Platform, VC Publisher, Center Denmark Energy Platform, and GLayer Server, interacting with front-end components such as VC Map and Dashboards. (D2.1 sec 3.1, D1.3 sec 3.4) - Data Hub and Catalogue: A "Data Hub Civora" and the "BIPED Digital Twin" form a central hub for data. The Data Catalogue facilitates the import of static data files. (D2.1 sec 3.1 and D1.3 sec 3.6) - Model Integration and Execution: The Model Coordinator component enables the integration of models hosted on different platforms via APIs. The "Data Routing API" manages models and processes by defining inputs, outputs, and endpoint details, effectively creating a pipeline for executing these models. The first release includes the integration of an energy model (District Heating Load Forecasting Model) and two mobility models (Macroscopic Traffic Modelling and Environmental Impacts Modeling). (D2.2 table 3 and D2.1 sec 3.1) - Communication Protocols: The system utilizes messaging protocols such as AMQP and MQTT, and communication via REST APIs and OGC APIs, which are standard for data exchange and pipeline orchestration. (D1.3 sec 3.3 and D2.1 sec 3.1). Other datasources are expected in near future, meaning the list of protocols might be extended.

Question: What kind of visualizations is your LDT supporting? Answer: The BIPED LDT supports various visualizations to present urban data and model outputs: - Front-End Components: The LDT utilizes "Dashboards" and a "VC Map" as primary front-end components for visualization (D2.1 sec 3.4). - Specific Examples: - Traffic Simulation: Visualizations show traffic congestions, often represented as red line segments. (D2.2 sec 5.2) - Solar Potential Analysis: This is visualized using a red-to-green color scale, where red indicates high potential and green indicates low potential. (D2.2 sec. 5.2) - Traffic Speed Dashboard: A GLayer traffic speed dashboard specifically for Aarhus provides information on average speeds, average travel times, and sample sizes for selected road segments and times. This dashboard uses TomTom Traffic Stats data. (D2.2 sec 5.2) - Innoconnect daskboard: building occupancy in Aarhus

The CitCom marketplace is where the participants of the FIWARE data space publish their datasets and services, and where other organisations find and buy them. It is the place to find what is available: the datasets and services of every participant, with their descriptions and terms of use.

Open the marketplace

Anyone can browse it. To buy or to publish, your organisation must join the data space, and its legal representative logs in with a wallet.

docs.title: How the marketplace is organised
docs.text:
• Services lists every offer of every provider, datasets and web services alike.
  • Catalogues group the offers by provider.
  • Categories are shared by the whole data space, so the filters work the same for every provider. The data space operator adds a category when a new kind of offer needs one.
  • The home page shows the offers that have an image.

Each offer describes itself: what it contains, how to access it and its terms of use. This site does not keep a copy of the list: the marketplace is the only inventory.

docs.title: Buying an offer
docs.text:
1. Log in with the wallet of your organisation's legal representative.
  2. Open the offer, read its description and terms of use, and buy it.
  3. When the order is completed, the provider's connector applies the contract on its own: it trusts your organisation's credentials and loads the access policy of the offer. See the purchase flow.

Then:

  • for a dataset, your programs read it with a MachineCredential: Use data from your code;
  • for a web service, the people of your organisation open it with their wallet and a ServiceCredential with the service's role: Get a wallet and your credentials.

docs.title: MIAIS: build an interoperable service
docs.text:
The Minimal Interoperable AI Service (MIAIS) is a small AI service that plans waste collection routes. It is deliberately simple: its value is not the algorithm, but showing what changes in a service when it climbs the interoperability levels, from a custom integration with one city to a service of the data space that any city can use.

Repository Try it in the marketplace

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The MIAIS reads the waste containers of a city (WasteContainer entities, with their location and filling level), lets the user choose the ones above a filling level, and computes the routes of the trucks with the Openroute optimisation service (VROOM).

flowchart LR
    UI["Web UI<br/>map and filters"] --> SRV["server.py<br/>Flask"]
    SRV --> DS["DataSource<br/>reads the containers"]
    SRV --> OPT["Optimization<br/>routes"]
    DS --> SRC[("Containers<br/>depends on the level")]
    OPT --> ORS["Openroute"]

Only one piece depends on the interoperability level: where DataSource gets the containers from. The rest of the service never changes.

docs.title: The three levels, one branch each
docs.text:
Level Branch Where the containers come from Access 0 · Custom integration valencia The Valencia platform, with its own authentication and its own tenant and service path A user of that platform 1 · NGSI-LD + Smart Data Models mvs-orionld, mvs-scorpiold Any NGSI-LD broker. The branches bring a local one with sample data Open 1 and 2 · Data space master Any NGSI-LD broker (level 1) or the provider's connector (level 2), by configuration None, or a MachineCredential

master is the current version and the one to start from. The other branches are kept to show the steps.

docs.title: Level 0 → 1: from one platform to a standard
docs.text:
At level 0, the service speaks the dialect of one platform. Reading the containers of Valencia needs a token of the city's identity server, its tenant (service) and the service path where the containers are:

server.py · branch valencia (level 0)
def get_all_WasteContainers():
    service = "tef_vlci"
    subservice = "/residuos_contenedores_vlc"

    auth = Authv2()
    token = auth.get_auth_token_subservice(service, subservice)

    context = os.environ.get("WASTECONTAINERS_CONTEXT")
    containers = client.get_all_entities_by_type(
        "WasteContainer", context, 100, 0, service, subservice, token).json()
    return containers

At level 1, all of that disappears. The service asks any NGSI-LD broker for WasteContainer entities, described with the Smart Data Model:

server.py · branch mvs-orionld (level 1)
def get_all_WasteContainers():
    context = os.environ.get("WASTECONTAINERS_CONTEXT")
    containers = client.get_all_entities_by_type("WasteContainer", context).json()
    return containers

The proof: mvs-orionld and mvs-scorpiold have exactly the same code. They only differ in the broker that docker compose starts (Orion-LD or Scorpio) and its port. Two brokers from different vendors, one service.

docs.title: Level 1 → 2: add a credential, not a new integration
docs.text:
At level 2 the data comes from another organisation, through its data space connector. The API is still NGSI-LD, so the query is the same. The only addition is a token of the data space on every request, which ds-consumer-auth provides as a ready-made HTTP session. FiLiP is the NGSI-LD client:

services/DataSource.py · branch master (level 1 and 2)
class DataSource:
    def __init__(self):
        self.url = os.environ.get("NGSI_LD_URL", "http://localhost:1026")

        session = None
        if os.environ.get("DS_ISSUER_URL"):  # level 2
            from ds_consumer_auth import data_space_session

            session = data_space_session()

        self.client = ContextBrokerLDClient(url=self.url, session=session, ...)

    def waste_containers(self):
        return self.client.get_entity_list(entity_type="WasteContainer", limit=100)

Whether the service runs at level 1 or level 2 is a matter of configuration:

Level 1: a brokerLevel 2: the CitCom data space 
NGSI_LD_URL="http://localhost:1026"

NGSI_LD_URL="https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/lepus"
# credential of the consumer (VRAIN), issued by its own Keycloak
DS_ISSUER_URL="https://keycloak-vrain.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/realms/provider"
DS_USERNAME="<machine user of your organisation>"
DS_PASSWORD="<its password>"
# verifier of the provider (Ajuntament de València)
DS_VERIFIER_URL="https://verifier-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/services/machine-id"
DS_SCOPE="operator1"

The real work of level 2 is outside the code: the consumer's organisation must have bought the offer in the marketplace. Until then, the provider's verifier rejects the credential. See the purchase flow.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Level 1, on your machineLevel 2, against the data space

You need Docker, Python 3.12 and a free Openroute API key.

git clone https://github.com/CitComAI-Hub/waste-collection-demo.git
cd waste-collection-demo
docker compose up -d          # Orion-LD on http://localhost:1026, empty
python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env          # set OPENROUTESERVICE_API_KEY
set -a && source .env && set +a
flask --app server run        # http://127.0.0.1:5000

The broker starts empty. Create some WasteContainer entities with a location and a fillingLevel first; the branch mvs-orionld has a script with sample data (upsert_fake_data.py).

  1. Your organisation joins the data space and has a machine user in its Keycloak.
  2. Its LEAR buys the Waste containers offer of the Ajuntament de València in the marketplace.

  3. Set the level 2 variables above in .env and run it as in level 1, or with Docker:

    docker build -t waste-collection-demo .
docker run --rm -p 5000:5000 --env-file .env waste-collection-demo

If /wastecontainers answers 502 with the verifier rejected the credential, the purchase is missing or not completed. The guide Use data from your code covers the errors.

docs.title: Offer it as a service
docs.text:
VRAIN runs the MIAIS for everyone and offers it in the marketplace as Access to the MIAIS Waste Collection. An organisation buys it, and its people log in with a wallet: no accounts, no passwords.

  • The web is published behind VRAIN's connector gateway, which handles the wallet login and checks the access policy.
  • The service asks for its own role, waste_collection_user, in the person's ServiceCredential. The buyer's organisation gives that role only to the people who use the service.
  • The app runs under a path prefix (/waste-collection/), so it uses relative URLs.

The guide Publish a web service explains how to do the same with your service.

docs.title: Build your own
docs.text:
To turn your own service into an interoperable one, follow the same steps:

  • Model your data with Smart Data Models. Look for an existing model in smartdatamodels.org before creating one.
  • Read and write through NGSI-LD, with a client such as FiLiP. Keep all access to the data in one class, like DataSource.
  • Take every endpoint from configuration, never from the code: broker URL, tenant, entity type.
  • Test at level 1 against a local Orion-LD and a local Scorpio. If it works with both, it does not depend on a vendor.
  • Add the data space session with ds-consumer-auth, activated by configuration.
  • Package it as a Docker image with a versioned tag, a health check and no secrets inside.
  • If it has a web UI, use relative URLs, so it works behind a path prefix.
  • Offer it in the marketplace: as data, with Publish a dataset, or as a service, with Publish a web service.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The testing zone is located in Brussels, Belgium and is centred around innovations for dynamic traffic management and traffic sensor solutions. The leading partner is the region of Brussels' transport authority Bruxelles Mobilité, supported by Paradigm, FARI, imec and Digitaal Vlaanderen.

The Charles Quint avenue and Annie Cordy tunnel are offered as primary testing location. Charles Quint is a major entry axis connecting the ring road of Brussels with its city center, the Annie Cordy tunnel is an extention to this axis. This axis provides an interesting and challenging traffic situation, common for large cities. Incidents (or measures) can have a profound and cascading effect on the entire regional traffic. The testing zone consists of: - 9 crossings - 1 tunnel, 2.9 km long - making it the longest tunnel in Belgium

Along the entire acis, multiple sensors and technologies are deployed to monitor and act upon the traffic situation. Innovators are offered access to the data these sensors produce to create, test and improve their solutions, e.g. validating their models or calibrate their sensors. Technologies that are currently deployes on the avenue are (or will be) offered through the TEF. - ANPR cameras - XStream cameras - Traffic light controllers - Magnetometers - DAI (automatic incident detection) cameras - Air quality sensors - and more...

All data is offered to innovators through the regional data platform.

Last but not least, innovators are also offered the ability to temporarily deploy their novel (traffic) sensors and / or solutions on the avenue.

  • Deploy and test traffic solutions: Temporary deployment of your solution or sensor in a real-life dynamic situation (the Charles Quint avenue or Annie Cordy tunnel)
  • Integrate traffic solutions: Integrate your solution for testing purposes and have it used by Bruxelles Mobilité's traffic operators. Receive real-life validation, feedback and / or recommendations by end-users and validate your solution's effectiveness and / or accuracy.
  • CAVE: CAVE or Computer Augmented Virtual Environment is a state-of-the-art immersive space that can visualize and simulate digital content and virtual objects to mimic real-world phenomena.
  • Local Digital Twin scenario development: Develop a digital twin of a city, building or environment or employ the digital twin to simulate scenarios (e.g. on traffic, resilience, ...)

docs.text: The French test site is located in the Paris region at 5 dedicated sites (Trappes, Satory, Linas, Saclay and Champs-sur-Marne) and is dedicated to advancing research and development in autonomous mobility. This site is equipped with state-of-the-art infrastructure (test tracks, XiL simulation test bench...) and is a key site in the CitCom.ai project, facilitating the integration and validation of its high-risk AI devices to help them integrate into the urban environment.

docs.title: Services Offered
docs.text:
• Virtual facility services: The French node can cover all simulation needs (HIL, MIL, SIL, DIL, VIL) for the virtual design of transport systems and vehicles, evaluating multimodal Human-Computer Interactions, AI evaluation, driving simulation, intelligent sensors evaluation...
  • Physcial facility services: We will provide test tracks for tests as close as possible to real conditions (urban or suburban traffic areas, urban road infrastructure, etc.) for example at UTAc with TEQMO or UGE at Satory. They will also be able to draw on the approval and certification expertise and the upstream research expertise to support them, depending on their stage of development. We can also provide the full range of regulatory test benches for vehicle certification (Charging, battery, EMC, acoustic, emission, ...) or sensor characterization physical bench in addition to track tests.

The UGE will also be able to make available the Sense-City physical test facility that allows controlled weather conditions in a bench simulating a small urban area. \

The UGE provides the real design of transport systems and vehicles, thanks to the ImPACT 3D AV which is a real automated vehicle for the prototyping, testing and evaluation of automated or communicating systems. This real prototype will make it possible to study, among other things, the impact of new technologies on the environment. ImPACT 3D AV embed a full hardware architecture with various sensor technologies to test algorithms on tracks

  • Algorithm creation & validation: The French node will be able to carry out customised testing of all AI algorithms on software-in-the-loop benches for urban mobility applications. From the conceptualisation of the test plan, to the creation of the database (Tests can be carried out by simulation or using real data), to the choice or creation of metrics and tools, all the parameters for evaluating algorithms can be discussed.

In an upstream approach, IRT SystemX offers one of its reference technological platforms: DebiAI, open source platform for improving the quality of datasets and their use in learning models. This platform provides support in the specialisation of the data necessary for a use case and the representativeness of the data available or used.

We also offer cybersecurity tests.

  • Compliance & ethics assistance: The LNE (the oldest body dedicated to AI evaluation in Europe) can also help innovators obtain certification or regulatory support for their AI algorithms (the LNE was the first in the world to provide a process certification for IA solution). The LNE can also accompany on the ethical aspects and preparation to the AI Act. At UTAC, we can also provide the full range of regulatory test benches for vehicle certification (Charging, battery, EMC, acoustic, emission, ...). UTAC has developed its own certification focused on autonomous vehicles. Potential customers can also access the UTAC and LNE training catalogue on AI and autonomous vehicles

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Center Denmark is located in Fredericia, Denmark, and serves as a national hub for digitalization across the utility sector. As a TEF Site in the CitCom.ai project, Center Denmark focuses on enabling AI-driven innovation by providing access to high-quality, real-world data from electricity, water, and heating systems (including gas and PtX where relevant).

Center Denmark provides secure and structured data infrastructure that supports collaboration between utilities, AI innovators, and researchers. The site plays a central role in bridging the gap between data availability and AI application by making validated utility datasets accessible for development, testing, and scaling of smart solutions that support the green transition.

In short: Center Denmark provides access to high-quality utility data through a dedicated data portal, offering both downloadable datasets and API-based access – ready for use in AI, analytics, and research.

docs.title: Services Offered
docs.text: The following services provided by Center Denmark as part of the CitCom.ai ecosystem are focused on enabling secure, structured, and value-driven access to utility data. Whether for collaboration between utilities and service providers, academic research, or early-stage experimentation, the services make it possible to work with real-world data from electricity, water, heating, gas, and PtX – all compliant with GDPR and tailored to different needs.

docs.title: Available Services and Example Datasets
docs.text:
Center Denmark builds customised datasets based on specific needs and can also provide predefined datasets for common use cases. To create tailored datasets, the platform combines a wide range of trusted data sources from utilities and public registers, ensuring they are structured, cleaned, and ready for use in AI training, research, forecasting, or infrastructure planning.

In addition to customised datasets, Center Denmark offers predefined datasets representing some of the most frequently requested data domains:

  • District Heating Data – time-series consumption and production data, typically aggregated to daily values.
  • Water Data – metered water consumption datasets, supporting both operational and analytical applications.
  • Electricity Data – household or aggregated consumption data, enabling load analysis, forecasting, and optimization use cases.

A full overview of available data sources and datasets can be explored via portal.centerdenmark.com or in the Data Catalouge.

docs.title: Service 1: Access to Utility Data for Co-developed Digital Services
docs.text:
This service supports collaboration between utility companies and service providers by granting access to structured and enriched utility data. The data is typically used for AI and analytics purposes such as forecasting, predictive maintenance, or grid planning. Center Denmark manages the entire data process – from collection and cleansing to enrichment and delivery – ensuring high data quality and full GDPR compliance.

docs.title: Service 2: Build-Your-Own Utility Dataset
docs.text:
This modular service enables data consumers (e.g. researchers, startups) to configure and request customized datasets based on available utility data. Users select a base dataset (electricity, water, heating) and can combine it with open data sources such as weather data, building information (BBR), electricity spot prices, or demographic data. The final dataset is delivered at the desired processing level (e.g. anonymised or pseudonymised), and pricing depends on the complexity and scope of the request.

docs.title: Service 3: Open Utility Datasets
docs.text:
This service provides free access to pre-approved, anonymised datasets via Center Denmark’s data portal. It is designed for early-stage experimentation, prototyping, education, and exploratory analysis. The datasets are ready to use and can be combined with publicly available data sources such as weather and building data, without any need for customization.
