docs.text:
• Data Platforms: Data is available from Center Denmark’s secure data platform, providing structured, GDPR-compliant datasets from utilities and public sources. Data can be accessed via RESTful APIs or by downloading datasets through the Data Portal (portal.centerdenmark.com).
  • Local Digital Twins: Center Denmark does not deliver a digital twin itself but provides the data infrastructure and standardized interfaces (aligned with Smart Data Models format) that enable third parties to build digital twins on top of the platform.
  • Specific Hardware: No physical sensors or field devices are operated directly by Center Denmark. Data is sourced from utility partners’ smart meters, SCADA/SRO systems, and IoT devices. High-performance compute resources and secure servers are used for data ingestion, processing, and structuring.
  • IoT Platforms: Data streams from IoT sources, such as smart meters, SCADA systems, weather stations, and building sensors, are securely integrated via partner-provided connections and standardized for use on the platform.
  • Visualization Platforms: Visualization is primarily based on open-source tools such as Apache Superset, offering flexible dashboards and analytics. The platform also supports integration with Power BI and other external visualization environments as needed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Milano TEF site belongs to the south supernode. It includes two key locations: the UpTown District from Euromilano and the Olympic Village from Covivio. Both areas sit at the heart of major urban regeneration projects, where public and private stakeholders work together to deliver new buildings that blend housing, commercial, and recreational facilities to improve quality of life and promote environmental sustainability. The UpTown District rises in the Cascina Merlata area of Milano, the former Expo 20215 venue. It is a modern neighborhood that hosts over 15,000 residents, with housing and services integrated into the urban fabric. One of Milano's largest parks surrounds the area, offering 300,000 square meters of green space rich in biodiversity. The Olympic Village is taking shape in Porta Romana, a central district of Milano. It will host athletes during the 2026 Winter Olympic Games before being repurposed for student housing and public use. These two sites offer a unique opportunity: test advanced AI in the city's heart. From automated monitoring and predictive maintenance to energy optimization, urban planning, and biodiversity tracking, the UpTown District and Olympic Village serve as real-world labs for intelligent facility management at the metropolitan scale.

Politecnico di Milano, Italy's top-ranking technical university, leads the site through the joint work of two departments: DEIB, focused on electronics and information technology, and ABC, focused on architecture, built environment, and construction engineering. Two key partners ensure a direct connection with the urban landscape. Euromilano, a real estate developer specializing in urban regeneration, manages the UpTown testing areas, providing practical integration of AI solutions in real estate and infrastructure projects. Covivio contributes expertise in sustainable urban development and innovative facility management.

The Milano TEF site is part of the CitCom.ai project. It features state-of-the-art infrastructure, facilitating collaboration between cities and communities, industrial partners, and research institutions and bringing AI innovation into everyday urban operations. By combining AI-driven sensor networks, facility automation, and edge/cloud computing solutions, the Milano TEF enables real-world validation of AI technologies, unlocking long-term regeneration projects, boosting sustainability, improving quality of life, and strengthening collaboration between academia, industry, and public stakeholders.

docs.title: IT Services
docs.text:
• Embedded AI/IoT Sofware Design and Development: design and development of embedded AI/IoT software for sensing, computing, and communication; including hardware-specific customization. Not necessarily customer-facing.
  • Networking IoT Devices: design and deployment of low-power wireless sensing technologies, for example, LoRAWAN, including network planning and operation testing. Not necessarily customer-facing.
  • Edge and Cloud Deployment: design and development of edge and cloud software, possibly including concrete operation on Politecnico's data center, enabling efficient and large-scale execution of AI processing. Not necessarily customer-facing.
  • Time Series Storage and Sharing: storage and sharing of temporal data from client-specified or public sources, enabling accesses on time series datasets.
  • FIWARE Big Data Processing: deployment of our FIWARE custom component that enables aggregation and computation of custom metrics based on big data collected from sensors.
  • Large-scale Distributed Sensing: design and deployment of large scale distributed sensing facilities, accounting for requirements of the deployment locations where specific sampling may be necessary.
  • Bare-metal Compute: deployment and access to a bare-metal computing infrastructure hosted in Politecnico di Milano, which provides full control on infrastructure configuration, components, and offers various customization options.

docs.title: Facility Management Services
docs.text:
• Integration of Facilities in Terms of Management: creation of a framework for tender documents, which includes a comprehensive needs analysis developed using the Kano model to help define priorities for public administrations, asset owners, building managers, and facility managers. The framework supports the preparation of tenders for the integrated management of building facilities and neighborhoods. By unifying facilities under a single tender, it enables more efficient service delivery and better coordination across different operational areas.
  • Global service approach: creation of a detailed inventory of all services provided by the project’s creators and providers, grouping them into services for individuals, businesses, and buildings or neighborhoods. This structured mapping unlocks the identification of the services that align best with the needs of key clients such as Facility Management companies, Asset Management firms, Property companies, Utility providers, and Municipalities.
  • Feasibility of the implementation of a service for the Italian market: study of the legal and technical, feasibility of implementing client's services designed and tested abroad for the Italian market. This enables the creation of a framework for local testing and certification path, if required. The service will be provided considering the time-cost-quality triangle.
  • Market Attractiveness Study of Services for the Italian Market: study of the commercial and market viability of the client's services for the local Italian market.

  • Data visualization: Grafana, Apache2 webserver with custom web pages
  • Data transmission and interconnection: MQTT, The Things Network (LoRaWAN), FIWARE
  • Data processing and automations: NodeRED, Apache Spark
  • Database: InfluxDB, MySQL/MariaDB, MongoDB
  • AI Tools: Tensorflow, PyTorch

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Milano TEF infrastructure enables seamless integration and real-time processing of IoT data across multiple urban deployment sites located in Italy. The sensors deployed in Cascina Merlata, Porta Romana, and the Mithraeum of Rome transmit data using heterogeneous communication protocols (MQTT, ZenoH, and LoRaWAN via The Things Network). Data incoming from our site locations is unified by corresponding FIWARE IoT Agents and delivered to a central FIWARE Context Broker, representing our infrastructure's central data exchange location. Our infrastructure supports reliable data storage (InfluxDB, MongoDB), continuous analytics, data aggregation using our custom streaming component (EsperTech), and access through Traefik and authentication layers. Finally, visualization and analysis tools (Grafana, Spark, Node-RED, Snap4City) enable real-time monitoring of our infrastructure and allow end users to extract environmental conditions insights, urban infrastructure usage, and system health.

docs.title: Relevant datasets of the site
docs.text:
Milano TEF site offers the following datasets:

  • Air quality: air quality readings from sensors deployed across the Milano area, reporting temperature, humidity, and pollutant levels along with time and location.
  • Biodiversity: data from biodiversity sensors deployed in UpTown, reporting device status, energy levels, and bird species detections over time.
  • Energy distribution: data from heating systems deployed in UpTown, reporting energy use, fluid temperatures, and heating power.
  • Archaeological site: environmental data from sensors deployed in an underground archaeological site, reporting air quality, temperature, humidity, and vibration levels over time.

docs.text:
1. Download or clone repository.
  2. Run pip install -r requeriments.txt + Enter.
  3. Run the deploy.sh file, which deploys each service independently:
  4. The logging (external) can be consulted at WhyLabs.

docs.title: Previous considerations
docs.text:
For the operation of the Logging and Monitor modules, the ones exposed in this repository, it is necessary a database that stores the predictions and revisions in the expected way, this is:

  • filename: (string) base name of the image.
  • output_confidence: (float) (optional) confidence of the max class predicted.
  • output_prediction: (int) predicted class.
  • output_validated: (bool) if it is validated the prediction.
  • timestamp: (string/timestamp) timestamp of the prediction.
  • trained: (bool) (optional) if it is already used for retraining.
  • logged: (bool) if is is already logged to the external logging.
  • timestamp_validated: (string/timestamp) timestamp of the validation.

A MongoDB has been used in the implementation. If you wish to use another database, it would be necessary to update the corresponding part of the code, maintaining the described structure.

docs.title: Logging (External)
docs.text: The Logging module tracks the model's performance in production. It logs various performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and the number of predictions made over time. A monitoring platform visualizes these metrics, helping identify trends and potential issues. Additionally, this module monitors the system for any anomalies or significant drops in performance, triggering alerts when necessary to ensure the model remains reliable and any problems are promptly addressed.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
Key features of the module include performance logging, drift detection, data storage, and scheduling.

  • Performance logging involves logging various aspects of the classification model's performance.
  • Drift detection identifies any changes in the model's performance over time.
  • Data storage ensures that logged performance metrics and related metadata are stored in a database, providing a robust system for retrieving and analyzing historical performance data.
  • A scheduler ensures regular monitoring tasks, ensuring continuous and timely monitoring of the model's performance.

docs.title: Functionalities
docs.text:
The module's functionalities include environment configuration, database connection, monitoring tasks, scheduler initialization, and error handling.

  • Environment configuration involves setting environment variables for the monitoring platform.
  • Database connection uses the provided URI and database name to establish a connection to the database, ensuring reliable database access.
  • The monitoring task fetches new entries from the database and logs their performance metrics, integrating with the logging platform to create and store performance logs.
  • Scheduler initialization sets up a blocking scheduler to run the monitoring task regularly, ensuring the monitoring process runs continuously without manual intervention.
  • Error handling entails logging errors encountered during database connection and monitoring tasks, and providing feedback on the status of the monitoring process.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The module has been implemented using WhyLogs and WhyLabs. WhyLogs is a logging library that captures various performance metrics, and WhyLabs is a platform that helps identify trends and potential issues.

docs.title: Monitor (Internal)
docs.text: The Monitor module is designed to track the performance of the classification model in production. Using charts, it provides a web interface that visualizes various performance metrics over a selected time range. The module utilizes a web framework for the backend, a database for data storage, and a charting library for creating interactive charts.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
Key features of this module include a web interface, data fetching, and charts.

  • The web interface allows users to monitor model performance through various tabs.
  • Data fetching retrieves logs based on user-specified date ranges, and performance metrics such as precision, accuracy, recall, and F1 score are calculated.
  • Interactive charts visualize these metrics, including line charts for overall metrics and bar charts for class-specific metrics.

docs.title: Functionalities
docs.text:
The detailed functionalities include environment configuration, database connection, metrics calculation, chart initialization, and web interface tabs.

  • Environment configuration involves setting up connection details for the database.
  • A connection to the database is established using the provided URI and database name, and data is fetched based on the user-specified date range.
  • Metrics calculation computes daily precision, accuracy, recall, and F1 score, which are then aggregated to provide an overall performance view.
  • Chart initialization visualizes these metrics, with line charts for daily metrics and bar charts for metrics by class.

docs.title: Web interface tabs
docs.text:
The web interface includes several tabs:

  • The main tab provides an overview of the validated samples and metrics.
  • The metrics tab displays separate line charts for precision, accuracy, recall, and F1 score.
  • The samples by class tab features a pie chart of validated samples by class.
  • The metrics by class tab displays bar charts of precision, recall, and F1 score by class.
  • The training data tab includes a pie chart of samples by class from the training dataset.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The module has been implemented using Flask and Chart.js, a JavaScript library for creating interactive charts.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
Additionally, other libraries and platforms were considered:

  • Evidently, a tool for evaluating and monitoring the performance of machine learning models, providing detailed reports and visualizations of model metrics.
  • Grafana + Prometheus, where Grafana is an open-source platform for monitoring and observability, providing dashboards and visualizations, and Prometheus is a monitoring system and time-series database that collects metrics and data.
  • alibi-detect, a library focused on detecting outliers, adversarial instances, and concept drift in machine learning models, ensuring the robustness and reliability of the deployed models.

docs.title: ds-consumer-auth
docs.text:
Repository

ds-consumer-auth is a Python library, made in CitCom, that gets the access token of a FIWARE data space for a program. It hides the whole credential flow behind a requests session: the token is obtained, cached, renewed before it expires, and a request that gets a 401 is retried once with a new token.

from ds_consumer_auth import data_space_session

session = data_space_session()  # configured with DS_* environment variables
response = session.get(
    "https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/lepus/ngsi-ld/v1/entities",
    params={"type": "WasteContainer"},
)

It works with any client built on requests, such as FiLiP.

docs.title: What it does for you
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant L as ds-consumer-auth
    participant KC as Your Keycloak
    participant VF as Provider verifier
    participant GW as Provider gateway
    L->>KC: Log in (machine user)
    L->>KC: Credential offer, pre-authorised code, token
    L->>KC: Credential request with proof of key possession
    KC-->>L: MachineCredential (SD-JWT, bound to the key)
    L->>VF: vp_token (credential + key binding)
    VF-->>L: Access token
    L->>GW: Requests with Authorization: Bearer

Steps 1 to 4 follow OID4VCI against Keycloak 26.6; the credential is valid for long and kept in memory. Step 5 presents it to the provider's verifier. Tested against the CitCom data space (FIWARE Data Space Connector 10).

docs.title: Install and configure
docs.text:
pip install "ds-consumer-auth @ git+https://github.com/CitComAI-Hub/ds-consumer-auth@v0.1.0"
Variable Required Description DS_ISSUER_URL yes Credential issuer of your organisation, e.g. https://keycloak-vrain.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/realms/provider DS_USERNAME, DS_PASSWORD yes Machine user that holds the credential DS_VERIFIER_URL yes Verifier service of the provider, e.g. https://verifier-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/services/machine-id DS_SCOPE no Scope asked to the verifier, e.g. operator1 DS_CREDENTIAL_TYPE no MachineCredential by default DS_HOLDER_KEY_FILE no Key of the holder, to keep the same one across restarts

The repository lists all of them.

From the shell, ds-token prints a token, handy to test with curl:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(ds-token)" "https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/ngsi-ld/v1/entities?type=TrafficState&limit=1"

docs.title: Before it works
docs.text: The provider's verifier only accepts your credential if your organisation bought one of its offers in the marketplace. The guide Use data from your code covers the whole process and the errors.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• One provider per session: create one session per provider.
  • Login with a user and password; client credentials and certificates are not supported yet.
  • Only for FIWARE data spaces. For Eclipse EDC, see the Eclipse EDC data space.

docs.title: Subscription of Orion Context Broker V2 to the IoT-Agent LD
docs.text:
Finally, a custom subscription is created in the V2 broker, in this way, for each modification of the values of a device, the broker will send a POST request (just like the previous one) in an automated way.

cURL (BrokerV2 -> IoT-Agent LD)

In the httpCustom:url, you cannot put addresses with -

curl -iX POST \
'http://ngsiv2.orion:1026/v2/subscriptions' \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-H 'fiware-service: vrainIoTA' \
-H 'fiware-servicepath: /' \
-d '{
    "description": "Reenvío datos entre brokers.",
    "status": "active",
    "subject": {
        "entities": [
            {
                "idPattern": ".*",
                "type": "example-type"
            }
        ],
        "condition": {
            "attrs": [],
            "notifyOnMetadataChange": true
        }
    },
    "notification": {
        "attrs": [],
        "onlyChangedAttrs": false,
        "attrsFormat": "normalized",
        "httpCustom": {
            "url": "http://ngsiv2.to-ngsild:7896/iot/json",
            "method": "POST",
            "headers": {
                "Content-Type": "application/json"
            },
            "qs": {
                "i": "${id}",
                "k": "vrainld2gpnvsb2uv4s40d59ov"
            },
            "json": {
                "t": "${temperature}",
                "h": "${humidity}",
                "f": "${fillingLevel}"
            }
        }
    }
}'
If everything goes well, we will receive a response like this: 
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Date: Thu, 02 Nov 2023 11:56:13 GMT
Fiware-Correlator: d244b742-7976-11ee-8fe6-0242ac130005
Location: /v2/subscriptions/65438e5d0a524d42d10bffca
Content-Length: 0

Analyzing in detail some elements of this request we have:

  • URL: Points to the subscriptions of the V2 broker.
  • fiware-service: Necessary for the subscription to work.
  • fiware-servicepath: Necessary for the subscription to work.
  • notification
    • attrs: There is no need to specify attributes as they are later selected in the body of the request.
    • httpCustom
      • url: Points to the IoT-Agent LD. Since the V2 broker network does not have direct visibility to the LD network, this address points to the reverse proxy between both networks.
      • qs:
        • k: The k parameter refers to the apiKey of the service in IoT-Agent of LD.
      • json: This is the body of the request. It relates the id of the attributes in the IoT-Agent LD (t, h and f) with the attributes in the V2 broker (${temperature}, ${humidity} and ${fillingLevel}).

docs.title: LDT Demonstrator
docs.text: The LDT Toolkit is not merely a collection of tools but a deployable demonstrator that integrates various open-source components to showcase advancements in interoperability, AI-readiness, and the practical implementation of Local Digital Twins (LDTs) in real-world scenarios.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
In the context of task 3.2, and more precisely related to the gap analysis performed by the Luxembourg TEF site, an evolution of its electromobility Local Digital Twin (LDT) is planned. This effort will culminate in the development of an LDT demonstrator which will be made available to showcase advancements in interoperability and AI-readiness.

The development process will follow several iterations, each aimed at progressively extending the digital twin's capabilities. These iterations align with the three twin models described in the section "Project Iterations & Twin Capabilities": the Descriptive Twin, the Predictive Twin, and the Prospective Twin. Each model builds upon the previous one, enhancing the ability to monitor, predict, and simulate real-world assets effectively.

The LDT demonstrator will be built using open-source components, ensuring transparency, accessibility, and community-driven development. Furthermore, it will align with the key standards and interfaces outlined in the EU LDT Toolbox, such as NGSI-LD and Smart Data Models, to guarantee interoperability and compliance with European frameworks.

docs.title: Lepus
docs.text:
Repository

Lepus serves the data of an NGSI-v2 context broker as NGSI-LD. It is the shortcut to interoperability level 1 for a city that already runs an NGSI-v2 platform: no migration, no copy of the data. Each NGSI-LD request is translated to NGSI-v2, sent to the platform, and the answer is translated back.

CitCom maintains a fork of the FIWARE Lepus, used by the Ajuntament de València to serve its VLCi platform in the data space.

flowchart LR
    C["NGSI-LD client"] -- "GET /ngsi-ld/v1/entities?type=WasteContainer" --> L["Lepus"]
    L -- "GET /v2/entities?type=WasteContainer<br/>Fiware-Service, Fiware-ServicePath, token" --> V[("NGSI-v2 broker")]
    V -- "NGSI-v2 entities" --> L
    L -- "NGSI-LD entities<br/>+ Smart Data Models @context" --> C

docs.title: What the CitCom fork adds
docs.text: Feature Why Keystone authentication Lepus gets its own token from the platform (Keystone v3), cached until it expires. The data space token of the client never reaches the platform. Tenant and service path NGSI-LD has no service path. Lepus deduces it from the entity type with a map, and uses a default tenant when the request has none. URN ids Platform ids that are not URNs (wastecontainer:6205…) are returned as urn:ngsi-ld:WasteContainer:wastecontainer:6205…, also with options=keyValues, and can be read back with that id. Smart Data Models @context Each entity comes with the @context of its Smart Data Models subject, e.g. dataModel.WasteManagement for WasteContainer. The list of models is downloaded once a day. Timeouts The timeouts to the platform apply to every request. Container image ghcr.io/citcomai-hub/lepus, one tag per release.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
Lepus is an HTTP service configured with environment variables; the main ones:

Variable Description NGSI_V2_CONTEXT_BROKER URL of the NGSI-v2 broker AUTH_URL, AUTH_USER, AUTH_PASSWORD Keystone of the platform, if it needs authentication LEPUS_DEFAULT_TENANT Tenant (Fiware-Service) when the request has no NGSILD-Tenant LEPUS_SERVICE_PATHS Map from entity type to service path NGSI_V2_PLAIN_IDS true if the platform ids are not URNs NGSI_V2_TIMEOUT Timeout of each request to the platform, in milliseconds

The repository has the full list, a docker compose setup to try it and Kubernetes manifests.

In a data space, place Lepus behind your connector's gateway like any other broker, on its own path, with the same token check and policy engine. In Valencia it is /lepus/ngsi-ld/*:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Accept: application/ld+json" \
  "https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/lepus/ngsi-ld/v1/entities?type=WasteContainer&limit=1"

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• It supports reading and writing entities, subscriptions, types, attributes and most batch operations; entityOperations/query and merge are not supported.
  • When an entity type lives in several service paths, only the first one is used.
  • Queries are as fast as the platform behind it: every request goes to the platform.

Another option: the IoT Agent

A FIWARE IoT Agent can also bridge NGSI-v2 and NGSI-LD, by copying the data through subscriptions. CitCom tested it and chose Lepus because it does not duplicate the data. See the IoT Agent experiment.

docs.title: NGSI-LD and FiLiP
docs.text: NGSI-LD is the API of MIM1: an ETSI standard to read, write and subscribe to data about real-world entities. Every entity has an id, a type and attributes, and a JSON-LD @context that gives the attributes their meaning, usually from Smart Data Models.

docs.title: The calls you need most
docs.text:
Call Does GET /ngsi-ld/v1/entities?type=WasteContainer&limit=100 List entities of a type GET /ngsi-ld/v1/entities?type=WasteContainer&q=fillingLevel>0.8 Filter by attribute GET /ngsi-ld/v1/entities/{id} One entity …&options=keyValues Only the values, without the NGSI-LD structure POST /ngsi-ld/v1/entityOperations/upsert Create or update several entities POST /ngsi-ld/v1/subscriptions Be notified of changes

Send Accept: application/ld+json to get the @context inside the body.

docs.text:
FiLiP (FIWARE Library for Python), by RWTH Aachen, is a Python client for FIWARE APIs, NGSI-LD included, with Pydantic models for the entities. CitCom uses it in the MIAIS.

pip install filip

cb = ContextBrokerLDClient(url="http://localhost:1026", fiware_header=FiwareLDHeader())

    url="https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu/lepus",

docs.title: Smart Data Models
docs.text:
Smart Data Models is the shared vocabulary of MIM2: open data models for smart cities, energy, environment, mobility and more, maintained by FIWARE, TM Forum, IUDX and OASC. A model fixes the entity type, the attribute names, their units and their meaning, and publishes a JSON-LD @context for NGSI-LD.

When two cities publish their waste containers as WasteContainer, a service written for one works with the other.

docs.title: Using a model
docs.text:
1. Search smartdatamodels.org for your entity before creating your own.
  2. Follow the model's schema.json for attribute names and types; the repository of each model has examples in NGSI-LD.
  3. Reference the @context of the subject (for example dataModel.WasteManagement) in your NGSI-LD requests, or let Lepus add it.
  4. If nothing fits, extend an existing model or contribute a new one.

atesta-id-wallet is a desktop wallet made in CitCom, in English, Spanish and Danish. Install it from the releases page: a Windows installer, a .deb for Debian and Ubuntu, or an AppImage for any Linux.

  • Add a credential: in your Keycloak account, Verifiable Credentials → Issue to wallet. Click the link, or press Scan QR and take a screenshot of the QR code.
  • Log in: click the login link, or press Scan QR and take a screenshot. Before sending anything, the wallet shows who is asking, where the data goes and which claims it will disclose. Nothing is sent until you press Share.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Uses the EUDI protocols, but it is not a certified EUDI Wallet

atesta-id-wallet uses the protocols of the European Digital Identity (EUDI) wallets: OpenID4VCI, OpenID4VP and SD-JWT VC. It is not a certified EUDI Wallet under eIDAS 2.0. That would need a provider notified by a Member State, certification at assurance level high, with a secure hardware key store, and wallet attestations, which are out of scope for this prototype.

  • Prototype (TRL 5), tested against Keycloak and the CitCom marketplace. Linux is the tested platform; the Windows builds are new and not yet tested by hand, and macOS is untested.
  • Software keys: the keys are kept encrypted on disk, not in a TPM or a secure element.
  • One holder key per profile: verifiers can correlate the presentations made with the same profile.
  • SD-JWT VC only (dc+sd-jwt, vc+sd-jwt): no jwt_vc_json, no mdoc, no deferred issuance.
  • Verifiers identified by X.509 certificates: verifiers identified by a DID, verifier attestations or OpenID Federation are not supported.
  • No revocation check of the credentials (Token Status List).

Read its security model before using it with real personal data.

docs.text: The guide Get a wallet and your credentials covers which credential you need, how to get it and the usual errors.

docs.title: Valencia: a city platform in the data space
docs.text:
The Ajuntament de València (City Council) was one of the first participants of the FIWARE data space. Its case is the reference for a city that already runs an urban platform and wants to offer that data to other organisations, without migrating the platform or copying the data.

Where the MIAIS shows the side of an AI service, this example shows the side of a data provider.

docs.title: The starting point
docs.text:
The city data lives in VLCi, the urban platform of the Ajuntament: an NGSI-v2 broker protected by Keystone, with its own data models. The goal was to reach interoperability level 2: the same data, as NGSI-LD with Smart Data Models, bought and accessed through the data space.

The steps were:

  1. Join the data space as the participant townhall-vlc, with its own connector. See Join the data space.
  2. Serve VLCi as NGSI-LD with Lepus inside the connector, so that VLCi stays as it is.
  3. Publish one offer per dataset in the marketplace, each limited to its entity type. See Publish a dataset.

docs.title: Data in the data space
docs.text:
The Ajuntament offers four datasets in the marketplace, one offer each, all as NGSI-LD with Smart Data Models:

Dataset Entity type Source Endpoint path Category Waste containers WasteContainer VLCi, through Lepus /lepus/ngsi-ld Waste management Air quality AirQualityObserved VLCi, through Lepus /lepus/ngsi-ld Environment Traffic flow TrafficFlowObserved VLCi, through Lepus /lepus/ngsi-ld Mobility Traffic state TrafficState VLCi open data /ngsi-ld Mobility

The endpoints are under https://apisix-townhall-vlc.citcom-vrain-dataspace.eu. Each offer gives access to its entity type only, with a MachineCredential. To use them, follow Use data from your code.

docs.title: How the data flows
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph CITY["Ajuntament de València"]
        VLCI[("VLCi platform<br/>NGSI-v2 + Keystone")]
        OD["Open data<br/>traffic state"]
    end
    subgraph TV["townhall-vlc connector"]
        GW["APISIX<br/>verifier token + ODRL policy"]
        LE["Lepus<br/>NGSI-LD → NGSI-v2"]
        OR[("Orion-LD")]
        EDC["Route for EDC<br/>OAuth2"]
    end
    CONS["Consumers of the<br/>FIWARE data space"]
    EDCC["Eclipse EDC<br/>data space"]

    CONS -- "/lepus/ngsi-ld" --> GW
    CONS -- "/ngsi-ld" --> GW
    GW --> LE --> VLCI
    GW --> OR
    OD --> OR
    EDCC -- "/edc/lepus/ngsi-ld" --> EDC --> LE
  • Lepus serves the VLCi data live. It translates each NGSI-LD query into NGSI-v2, authenticates with the city platform on its own, and returns the entities as NGSI-LD with their Smart Data Models @context. VLCi never sees the data space tokens, and nothing is copied. See Lepus.
  • APISIX protects every path with the same mechanism: a token from the verifier and the ODRL policy of the purchased offer.
  • The same Lepus also serves the Eclipse EDC data space, through its own route. See below.

docs.title: The same data in the Eclipse EDC data space
docs.text: Some CitCom partners use the Eclipse EDC data space instead. So that they can use the Valencia data too, the Ajuntament publishes the same source there, without copying it. The two data spaces stay separate: this is one provider making its data available in both.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
An EDC connector does not present verifiable credentials. To fetch an asset, its data plane calls a fixed HTTP address and authenticates with OAuth2 client credentials. The Ajuntament's FIWARE connector accepts exactly that on one dedicated route:

flowchart LR
    subgraph EDC["Eclipse EDC data space"]
        CONS["Consumer connector"] -- "DSP negotiation<br/>and transfer" --> PROV["Provider connector<br/>(asset)"]
    end
    subgraph TV["Ajuntament de València · FIWARE connector"]
        KC["Keycloak<br/>client edc-citcom"]
        GW["APISIX<br/>/edc/lepus/ngsi-ld/v1/entities"]
        LE["Lepus"]
    end
    VLCI[("VLCi platform<br/>NGSI-v2")]
    PROV -- "1 client credentials" --> KC
    KC -- "token (scope lepus-read)" --> PROV
    PROV -- "2 GET + token" --> GW
    GW --> LE --> VLCI
  1. The asset in the EDC data space points to the Ajuntament's gateway and holds an OAuth2 client of the Ajuntament's Keycloak.
  2. When a consumer has negotiated a contract for the asset, the provider's EDC data plane gets a token and reads the entities. The consumer receives them through EDC as usual.

The route is deliberately narrow:

  • It accepts only tokens with its own scope, which no other client of the realm has. A token for this route does not work on the rest of the connector, and the credentials-based tokens of the FIWARE data space do not work on this route.
  • It only allows GET on /entities, only for the entity types that are published, and with a rate limit.
  • It always returns JSON-LD, so the @context travels with the data.

Lepus is the same instance used in the FIWARE data space: both read the same, live data.

docs.title: What is published
docs.text: The Valencia datasets that Lepus serves can be published as EDC assets, one per entity type: WasteContainer, AirQualityObserved and TrafficFlowObserved. The bridge has been tested end to end: an EDC consumer negotiated a contract and downloaded the waste containers of Valencia through this route.

docs.title: Differences to keep in mind
docs.text:
FIWARE data space EDC data space Who is the consumer for the Ajuntament? Each organisation, by its DID The EDC connector that holds the asset Access rules ODRL policy per purchase, enforced by the Ajuntament's connector Contract policy in EDC; the Ajuntament's route only knows the client Queries Any NGSI-LD query The fixed address of the asset

In other words, in the EDC data space the access control between consumers happens in EDC. The Ajuntament's connector only trusts the EDC asset as a whole.

docs.title: Who uses this data
docs.text: Service Provider What it does MIAIS Waste Collection VRAIN Plans waste collection routes from the filling level of the Valencia containers. It reads the containers through the data space, and other organisations can use it by logging in with a wallet.

docs.title: Do the same in your city
docs.text:
• An NGSI-v2 platform: put Lepus in front of it, as here.
  • An NGSI-LD broker already: publish it directly through your connector.
  • Another kind of platform: see NGSI-LD and FiLiP and the other tools to bring it to NGSI-LD.

Then follow the guides from Get a wallet to Publish a dataset. The Valencia TEF site itself is described in TEF network.
